A person who is fluent in both languages and able to interpret accurately and impartially. A client's family member or minor child is not used except at the client's informed request, or in an emergency.

procedures: The administrator posts a short nondiscrimination statement in the office and includes it in the client packet. It lists who to contact with concerns: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] at [PHONE], and states that clients may also contact CDSS HCSB at (877) 424-5778.

At the intake visit, the intake coordinator asks and records the client's preferred spoken and written language, any hearing, vision, speech or cognitive communication needs, and any accommodation requests on the Intake Form (see SVC-02).

Intake and acceptance decisions are based on the client's care needs, safety, the licensed service area, the scope of services and aide availability. They are never based on a protected characteristic or source of payment. The reason for any declined referral is recorded in the intake log (see SVC-02).

If a client is not English-proficient, the office provides a qualified interpreter or telephone interpretation service at no cost to the client, and gives the Client Rights form, service agreement and service plan in the client's language when available or interprets them orally with documentation (see CR-01 and CR-06).

The agency does not require clients to supply their own interpreter. If a client chooses to use a family member, the aide or intake coordinator records the client's choice, and a qualified interpreter is used for matters involving safety, consent or complaints.

For clients with disabilities, the intake coordinator documents requested accommodations (such as large print, a reader, visual alerts, a service animal or flexible scheduling) and the supervisor decides within 3 business days (agency standard). If an accommodation cannot be provided, the administrator documents the reason and offers an effective alternative.

When matching aides to clients, the scheduler may consider client language and cultural preferences and aide skills, but never uses stereotypes. Client preference for an aide's protected characteristic is addressed case by case with the administrator, who ensures fair treatment of aides and clients.
Aides must not make discriminatory remarks, refuse care for discriminatory reasons or impose personal beliefs on clients. Violations are handled as misconduct under PER-07.

The administrator includes respectful, culturally competent care and communication access in the annual 'clients' rights' training and in orientation (see PER-03). The training log records attendance.
Any client, family member or employee who believes discrimination occurred may complain under CR-02. The administrator investigates within the same time frames and never allows retaliation.
Supervisors check at supervisory visits that language and accommodation needs are being met and update the service plan as needed (see SVC-03 and SVC-04).

The administrator reviews intake declines, accommodation requests and complaints quarterly for patterns and reports to the QA review under GOV-04. The policy is reviewed yearly under GOV-03, and counsel adds California law citations.

responsibilities.duty: Oversees nondiscrimination and language access, secures interpreter resources, decides difficult accommodation questions and reviews patterns.
Records language and accommodation needs, makes intake decisions on non-discriminatory grounds and arranges interpreters.
Matches aides and clients on skills, availability and documented needs without discrimination.
Verifies at visits that communication and accommodation needs are met and reports concerns.
Treat every client with respect, use interpreters as arranged and report discrimination concerns.

documentation: Posted nondiscrimination statement and client packet copy
Intake Form entries for language and accommodation needs
Intake log with reasons for declined referrals
Interpreter use records and translated documents provided
Accommodation requests and decisions
Training logs on clients' rights and culturally competent care
Complaint and investigation records (CR-02)

policies.title: Service Agreement, Rates and Billing Disclosure
policies.applies_to: Administrator, intake coordinator, client care supervisor, billing and scheduling staff
policies.purpose: To make sure every client or client representative receives a clear written agreement, with rates, cancellation terms, billing practices and complaint contacts, before services begin, and to prevent pricing practices that conflict with wage and hour law.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will give each client a written service agreement and obtain the client's or representative's signature before the first visit. The Home Care Services Consumer Protection Act does not prescribe the contents of a service agreement; the contents in this policy are the agency's own best-practice standard. The agreement will state the services, schedule, hourly rate, minimum visit length, cancellation terms, billing cycle, and how to complain to the agency and to CDSS. It will state that [AGENCY NAME] employs its aides (affiliated aides) and that they are registered with CDSS. Because a third-party employer such as an HCO may not claim the FLSA companionship or live-in exemptions (29 CFR §552.109), [AGENCY NAME] will not offer flat-rate live-in or 24-hour pricing until counsel has reviewed California overtime rules. For clients funded by a Medi-Cal managed care plan, rates and authorizations come from the plan contract, not from private-pay terms. Billing will match hours actually worked as recorded by the agency's timekeeping system.

definitions.definition: The written contract between [AGENCY NAME] and the client or the client's representative that describes the services, rates, billing and complaint process.
A registered home care aide who is employed by [AGENCY NAME] and listed on the CDSS Home Care Aide Registry.
The shortest visit, in hours, that the agency will schedule and bill for a client, as stated in the agreement.
A single price for a day or week of round-the-clock or overnight care that is not tied to hours worked. [AGENCY NAME] does not offer this pricing unless approved under this policy.
A client whose services are authorized and paid by a Medi-Cal managed care plan (for example, Community Supports Personal Care and Homemaker Services) under a contract with [AGENCY NAME].

procedures: The intake coordinator prepares the service agreement from the current approved template after the in-home assessment is complete (SVC-02) and before any aide is scheduled for a first visit.
The agreement lists the services to be provided using the permitted service categories in SVC-01, and the days, hours and start date of the schedule.
The agreement states the hourly rate, the minimum visit length, and every additional charge, if any. It must not contain any fee that is not written in it.
The agreement states the cancellation terms: how much notice the client must give, how the agency will give notice if it must cancel, and any charge for late cancellation.
The agreement states the billing cycle, invoice delivery method, payment due date and accepted payment methods.

The agreement states that [AGENCY NAME] employs the aides who will serve the client, that they are registered home care aides listed with CDSS, and that the client does not employ or pay the aide directly.

The agreement gives the client's complaint options: [AGENCY NAME] at [PHONE] and [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or designee; and CDSS Home Care Services Branch at (877) 424-5778 or HCSB@dss.ca.gov. It refers to the complaint process in CR-02.

The intake coordinator or care supervisor reviews the agreement with the client or representative in plain language, in the client's preferred language, using interpreter or translated materials as required by CR-05.

The client or representative signs and dates the agreement before services begin. The agency gives the client a complete copy and places the original in the client record. No visit is scheduled without a signed agreement.

Any live-in, overnight or 24-hour request is referred to the Administrator. Until counsel has reviewed California wage and overtime rules and the Administrator has approved in writing, staff quote only hourly rates for scheduled hours, and never a flat daily or weekly rate.

For a plan-funded client, the intake coordinator confirms the plan authorization (units, service type, dates) before the first visit. The agreement or an addendum refers to the plan authorization, and rates, billing and authorization limits follow the plan contract, not the private-pay rate sheet.

Staff do not bill a plan-funded client for services that the plan has authorized, or for amounts above the plan rate, unless the plan contract expressly allows it. Questions are referred to the Administrator.
Billing staff prepare invoices only from verified timekeeping records (SVC-07) and review each invoice for accuracy against the schedule and the agreement before it is issued.
Billing errors are corrected, and any overcharge is credited or refunded, within [BILLING CORRECTION DAYS] days of discovery. The correction is documented in the client's billing file.

Rate or term changes are made only by written amendment. The agency gives the client at least 30 days' written notice before a private-pay rate increase takes effect (operator standard), and the client or representative signs the amendment.
Billing disputes or complaints are logged and handled under CR-02. The Administrator reviews every unresolved billing dispute.
The Administrator reviews the service agreement template and rate sheet at least annually with counsel, under GOV-03.

responsibilities.duty: Approves the agreement template and rate sheet, approves any exception, reviews with counsel any live-in or 24-hour request, and reviews unresolved billing disputes.
Prepares the agreement, explains it, obtains signatures before services start, and verifies plan authorizations.
Helps explain services and schedule to the client and confirms the agreement matches the service plan.
Issues accurate invoices from verified timekeeping, applies correct payer rates and corrects errors.
Does not schedule a first visit until the signed agreement is on file.

documentation: Signed service agreement and any signed amendments, in the client record
Proof of delivery of the client's copy
Plan authorization and contract rate records for plan-funded clients
Counsel review and Administrator approval for any live-in or 24-hour arrangement
Invoices, billing corrections, credits and refunds
Billing complaint and dispute log entries

policies.title: Scope of Services — What Aides May and May Not Do
policies.applies_to: All aides, scheduler, client care supervisor, intake coordinator, Administrator
policies.purpose: To define the non-medical home care services that [AGENCY NAME] aides may perform under California law and to stop aides from performing services outside that scope.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides only non-medical home care services for clients who, because of advanced age or physical or mental disability, cannot perform the tasks themselves (HSC §1796.12(n)). Aides may provide bathing, dressing, feeding, exercising, personal hygiene and grooming, transferring, ambulating, positioning, toileting and incontinence care, assistance with self-administered medication, housekeeping, meal planning and preparation, laundry, transportation, correspondence, phone calls, shopping for personal care items or groceries, and companionship. Aides may not provide skilled nursing or therapy, may not administer medication, and may not give any medication help that would otherwise require administration or oversight by a licensed health care professional. Those services belong to home health agencies and other licensees (HSC §1796.17). Requests outside this scope are referred to the care supervisor, and no aide makes an exception in the field.

definitions.definition: Non-medical services provided to a client who cannot perform them because of advanced age or physical or mental disability, as listed in HSC §1796.12(n).
Medication that the client takes or applies on his or her own. The aide may assist only within the limits of SVC-05.
Nursing, therapy or other care that requires a licensed health care professional, such as wound care or injections. It is outside the agency's scope.
Any request from a client, family member or other person for a task that is not on the permitted list in this policy.

procedures: At orientation and each year, the care supervisor trains every aide on the permitted and prohibited services in this policy, and each aide signs an acknowledgment.
Before a client is accepted, the intake coordinator and care supervisor check that each need on the assessment falls within a permitted category (SVC-02).
The service plan lists tasks only by permitted category (SVC-03). The plan the aide receives is the only list of tasks the aide may do for that client.

Aides perform only the tasks on the service plan. If a client asks for a task not on the plan, even a permitted one, the aide explains kindly that the supervisor must approve it and calls the supervisor.

The aide may NOT perform skilled nursing or therapy, such as injections, wound or pressure-injury treatment, catheter care beyond what the licensed provider has set up, tube feeding or therapy exercises that a licensed professional must direct.

The aide may NOT administer medication or give any medication help that would otherwise require administration or oversight by a licensed health care professional. Follow SVC-05 for permitted medication assistance.

If a client or family asks for an out-of-scope task, the aide does not do it, even in an emergency that is not life-threatening. The aide calls the care supervisor right away. In a medical emergency, the aide calls 911 and follows SVC-08.

The care supervisor documents the request, decides whether the task can be included under a permitted category, and, if it cannot, tells the client or representative that the agency cannot provide it.
The care supervisor helps the client or representative find a licensed provider, such as the client's physician, a home health agency or another appropriate licensee, and documents the referral.
If the client's needs change so that the agency can no longer meet them within non-medical scope, the care supervisor follows SVC-08 and SVC-09 for referral, transition or discontinuation.
The scheduler does not assign an aide to any task that the service plan does not authorize.
The care supervisor reviews aide notes and complaints for out-of-scope activity. Any aide who performs an out-of-scope task is retrained, and repeated or serious violations are handled under PER-07.
The Administrator reviews out-of-scope requests and incidents quarterly under GOV-04 and updates training as needed.

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure the agency's services, advertising and agreements stay within the non-medical scope and reviews scope violations.
Trains aides on scope, decides on out-of-scope requests, makes referrals and documents each request.
Screens new clients for needs outside scope and explains scope to clients and families.
Perform only tasks on the service plan, decline out-of-scope tasks and call the supervisor.
Assigns aides only to tasks authorized on the service plan.

documentation: Signed aide acknowledgment of the scope policy
Out-of-scope request log and supervisor decision
Referral records to licensed providers
Service plans listing tasks by category
Retraining or corrective action records

policies.title: Client Intake, Eligibility and Assessment
policies.applies_to: Intake coordinator, client care supervisor, Administrator
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] accepts only clients whose needs can be safely met by non-medical home care, and to document each client's needs, risks and payer before services begin.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] accepts only clients whose needs can be met by non-medical home care within the agency's program description (CDSS HCS 281, Section B5). The Home Care Services Consumer Protection Act prescribes no assessment form or timeline. As the agency's own standard, the care supervisor completes an in-home assessment before the first visit. The assessment covers activities of daily living, cognition and dementia, mobility, home safety, medications used, emergency contacts, physician and representative, and language needs. Staff screen for needs that require a licensed provider, such as wounds, injections or skilled care, and refer those needs elsewhere (HSC §1796.12(n)). The agency confirms the payer before services begin: private pay, long-term care insurance, or Medi-Cal plan Community Supports (Personal Care and Homemaker Services). A client who receives IHSS may use the agency privately for hours beyond the IHSS authorization.

definitions.definition: A face-to-face evaluation of the client and home done by the care supervisor before services begin to identify needs, risks and preferences.
Basic self-care tasks such as bathing, dressing, eating, toileting, transferring and walking.
A person legally authorized or designated by the client to act for the client, such as an agent under a power of attorney or conservator.
The agency's description submitted to CDSS of its services, service area, hours, population, and how aides are assigned and supervised.

procedures: The intake coordinator takes the inquiry and records the caller's contact information, the client's name and location, the reason for care, the requested services and hours, and the payer.
The intake coordinator checks that the client's address is within the service area in the program description and that the agency has an aide available who can meet the request.

During the inquiry, the intake coordinator screens for needs outside the non-medical scope (SVC-01), including wounds, injections, skilled nursing or therapy needs. If found, the client is referred to an appropriate licensed provider, and the referral is documented.
The care supervisor schedules an in-home assessment before the first visit and invites the client's representative and family if the client wishes.

At the in-home assessment, the care supervisor documents ADLs, cognition and dementia concerns, mobility and fall risk, home safety hazards, medications the client uses, emergency contacts, physician, representative, and language and communication needs.
The care supervisor documents the client's preferences, routines, cultural needs, and any safety concerns for aides, including pets, weapons, smoking, and conditions in the home (SAF-06).

The care supervisor decides whether the agency can safely meet the client's needs. If it can, the supervisor writes the assessment summary. If it cannot, the intake coordinator tells the client or representative why, offers referrals, and documents the decision.

The intake coordinator confirms the payer: private pay, long-term care insurance, or Medi-Cal plan Community Supports. For plan-funded clients, the intake coordinator verifies the plan authorization before the first visit (SVC-10).

If the client receives IHSS, the intake coordinator confirms with the client that the agency's hours are private-pay hours in addition to the IHSS authorization. The agency does not bill IHSS or claim IHSS-authorized hours (SVC-10).
The intake coordinator reviews the client's rights and responsibilities and the privacy notice with the client or representative (CR-01, CR-03) and obtains the signed service agreement (CR-06).
The care supervisor writes the service plan from the assessment (SVC-03) before the first visit.
The intake coordinator opens the client record and files the inquiry form, assessment, referrals made, payer verification and signed forms (RR-01).
The care supervisor reassesses the client whenever the client's condition changes (SVC-08) and at each plan update (SVC-03).

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure admission decisions follow the program description and approves exceptions.
Completes the in-home assessment, decides if needs can be met, and writes the assessment summary.
Takes inquiries, screens for scope and service area, verifies payer and authorizations, and opens the client record.
Gives accurate health, medication, contact and home safety information.

documentation: Intake inquiry form
In-home assessment with date and assessor
Referral records for declined or out-of-scope needs
Payer verification and plan authorization records
Signed service agreement, rights notice and privacy acknowledgment
Assessment-to-service-plan transmittal

policies.title: Service Plan and Plan Updates
policies.applies_to: Client care supervisor, aides, scheduler, intake coordinator
policies.purpose: To make sure each client has a written service plan based on the assessment, that aides receive it before they work with the client, and that the plan is kept current.
policies.policy: The Home Care Services Consumer Protection Act sets no service plan content or review interval. As the agency's own standard, [AGENCY NAME] writes a service plan from the assessment for each client. The plan lists tasks by the home care service categories in HSC §1796.12(n), the schedule, the client's preferences and safety precautions. The aide receives the plan before the first visit, and an aide may be present with a client only after completing entry-level training (HSC §1796.44(b)). The plan is updated when the client's condition changes, at each supervisory visit when needed, and at least every 6 months (suggested interval). The client or representative signs each version.

definitions.definition: The written plan of tasks, schedule, preferences and safety precautions for a client, based on the assessment.

At least 5 hours of training before presence with a client: 2 hours of orientation on the aide's role and terms of employment, and 3 hours on safety (basic safety precautions, emergency procedures and infection control).
A dated, signed iteration of the service plan. Prior versions are kept in the record.

procedures: Within [PLAN DAYS] days of the assessment and before the first visit, the client care supervisor writes the service plan using the approved template.

The plan lists each task under a permitted category from SVC-01 (for example bathing, dressing, toileting, meal preparation, housekeeping, laundry, transportation, companionship), with how often and when it is to be done.

The plan records the client's preferences and routines, communication and language needs, mobility and transfer instructions, and safety precautions identified in the assessment, including fall risk and dementia-related concerns.
The plan records emergency contacts, the physician, the representative, and the emergency and disaster information in SAF-05.
The plan states the medication assistance the client may receive, limited to self-administration support as defined in SVC-05.
The supervisor reviews the plan with the client or representative. The client or representative signs and dates the plan, and receives a copy.

Before assigning an aide, the scheduler checks the aide roster to confirm the aide is registered, listed on the CDSS registry, and has completed entry-level training (PER-01, PER-03). An aide who has not completed the training is not assigned.
The supervisor gives the assigned aide the plan before the first visit and reviews it with the aide, including client-specific safety precautions. The aide signs that he or she has read the plan.
Aides follow the plan and report to the supervisor when the plan does not fit the client's needs. Aides do not change the plan themselves.

The supervisor updates the plan whenever the client's condition, needs or preferences change, after any hospitalization or incident (SVC-08, SAF-03), and when the client or representative requests a change.
The supervisor reviews the plan at each supervisory visit (SVC-04) and updates it if needed. At minimum, the supervisor does a documented review every 6 months.
Each updated plan is signed by the client or representative, given to the aide before the aide's next visit, and filed in the client record. Old versions are retained.

If the client or representative cannot sign, the supervisor documents why and how the client or representative agreed, such as a verbal agreement witnessed by a second staff member, and obtains a signature as soon as possible.
Any plan change that alters the agreement's hours, services or rates is also documented in an amendment under CR-06.

responsibilities.duty: Writes, reviews and updates plans, reviews them with the client and aide, and keeps the record current.
Read and follow the plan, and report changes in the client's condition and needs.
Assigns only registered aides who have completed entry-level training, and confirms the aide has received the plan.
Audits plans for completeness and timely updates under GOV-04.
Reviews, signs and requests changes to the plan.

documentation: Dated, signed service plan and every updated version
Aide acknowledgment of plan review
Documentation of 6-month and event-driven plan reviews
Entry-level training completion record checked before first assignment
Notes explaining any missing signature and follow-up

policies.title: Supervision of Caregivers and Supervisory Visits
policies.applies_to: Client care supervisor, aides, Administrator, scheduler
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME], as the employer of its aides, supervises caregivers and checks the quality and safety of care in each client's home.
policies.policy: The Home Care Services Consumer Protection Act sets no supervisor ratio, credential or supervisory-visit frequency. The agency's program description must state how aides are assigned and supervised (CDSS HCS 281, Section B5), and [AGENCY NAME] follows that description. CDSS has no oversight of individual registered aides beyond maintaining the registry (HSC §1796.52(d)), so the agency, as employer, is accountable for supervising its aides. As the agency's own operator standard, the client care supervisor makes a first-visit check within the first week of services, then supervisory visits or calls at least every 90 days, and documents each one.

definitions.definition: The agency employee designated by the Administrator to supervise aides and oversee client care: [CLIENT CARE SUPERVISOR NAME].
A visit or documented contact by the care supervisor within the first week of services to make sure the aide and the plan work for the client.
An in-home visit, or a documented call with the client or representative, to check aide performance, client satisfaction, plan accuracy and safety.

procedures: The Administrator designates in writing one or more client care supervisors and records their names, job descriptions and the clients they supervise. The designation is consistent with the program description.
The care supervisor assigns each aide to a client based on the client's needs, the aide's training and experience, language and preferences, and keeps the assignment in the client record.

Within the first week of services, the care supervisor makes a first-visit check, in person where possible, and documents the aide's performance, whether the plan fits, the client's satisfaction and any safety concerns.

At least every 90 days, the care supervisor makes a supervisory visit or documented call with the client or representative. At least one in-person visit is made when the client's condition, safety or complaints warrant it.

At each supervisory contact, the care supervisor checks that the aide follows the plan, performs only permitted tasks (SVC-01), assists with medication only as allowed (SVC-05), and maintains professional boundaries (PER-07).

The care supervisor asks the client or representative about satisfaction, rights concerns, missed or late visits, safety, and any signs of abuse, neglect or exploitation (SAF-01), and reviews the plan (SVC-03).
The care supervisor reviews the aide's timekeeping and visit notes for accuracy and consistency (SVC-07).
The care supervisor gives the aide feedback. Concerns are documented and addressed with coaching, retraining or corrective action under PER-07.
If the care supervisor finds suspected abuse, neglect, exploitation, an injury or other serious problem, the supervisor reports immediately to the Administrator and follows SAF-01 and SAF-03.
The care supervisor updates the service plan if the visit shows a change in the client's condition or needs, and notifies the scheduler of any assignment change.
The care supervisor documents each first-visit check and supervisory visit in the client record on the same day, including date, method (in person or call), who was contacted, findings and follow-up.
Each month, the Administrator reviews a report of supervisory visits due and completed. Any overdue visit is completed within [OVERDUE DAYS] days and the reason documented.
The Administrator reviews supervision results and complaints quarterly under GOV-04 and revises assignment and supervision practices as needed.

responsibilities.duty: Designates supervisors, keeps supervision consistent with the program description, and reviews the monthly supervisory visit report.
Assigns aides, makes first-visit checks and supervisory visits, coaches aides, updates plans and documents findings.
Take part in supervisory visits, follow supervisor direction and report problems promptly.
Tracks due dates for supervisory visits and informs the supervisor of upcoming deadlines.

documentation: Supervisor designation and job description
Aide-to-client assignment record
First-visit check form
Supervisory visit or call notes
Aide coaching and corrective action records
Monthly supervisory visit tracking report
Program description page stating assignment and supervision

policies.title: Medication Assistance and Self-Administration Support
policies.applies_to: All aides, client care supervisor, Administrator
policies.purpose: To define the limited medication assistance that aides may give, prevent aides from administering medication, and make sure errors and reactions are reported immediately.
policies.policy: Aides may assist only with medication that the client self-administers (HSC §1796.12(n)). Aides may not assist with medication that would otherwise require administration or oversight by a licensed health care professional. Those services belong to licensed providers (HSC §1796.17). The Act does not itemize allowed and forbidden acts, so [AGENCY NAME] defines them in the lists below, to be finalized by counsel and the care supervisor. Every assistance is recorded on a medication assistance log. Refusals are recorded, and errors, missed doses and adverse reactions are reported immediately.

definitions.definition: Medication that the client can take or apply on his or her own, with the client making the decision to take it and directing the process.
Verbal reminders and handing the client a container that the client opens and takes from.
Any act in which the aide decides, prepares, measures, gives or applies a medication, or otherwise takes control of medication that requires oversight by a licensed health care professional.
The record in the client's home or file of each time an aide helps with self-administered medication, including refusals.

procedures: At orientation and each year, the care supervisor trains aides on this policy, using the allowed and forbidden lists below, and each aide signs an acknowledgment (PER-03).

ALLOWED: giving a verbal reminder that it is time for the client to take medication; handing the client a medication container that the client opens; and observing and documenting that the client took the medication on his or her own.

FORBIDDEN: filling or setting up pill organizers; giving injections; adjusting or changing doses; crushing or splitting pills; giving PRN (as-needed) medications by the aide's judgment; applying medicated treatments that require clinical judgment; and any other act that administers medication or requires oversight by a licensed health care professional.

Before services begin, the care supervisor identifies the client's medications in the assessment (SVC-02) and decides whether the client can self-administer. If the client cannot self-administer and a licensed professional must oversee, the agency does not provide medication help, and the supervisor tells the client or representative and helps arrange a licensed provider.
The service plan describes the allowed medication assistance for the client and states that the aide may not do any forbidden act (SVC-03).
The aide helps only when the client is alert and able to make the decision to take the medication, and does not decide what, how much, or when the client takes medication.

The aide records each assistance on the medication assistance log on the same visit, with the date, time, medication name as shown on the container, what the aide did (reminder or handing the container), and whether the client took it.
If the client refuses, the aide does not persuade or force the client. The aide records the refusal on the log and tells the care supervisor by the end of the visit.

If the aide sees or suspects a medication error, a missed dose, an unusual reaction or a change in the client's condition, the aide calls the care supervisor immediately. If the client is in danger, the aide calls 911 first and then the supervisor (SVC-08).
The care supervisor contacts the client's physician or the client's representative as appropriate, advises the Administrator, and documents what was done. The incident is reported under SAF-03.
An aide who is asked to do a forbidden act declines, explains that the agency cannot do it, and calls the care supervisor. The supervisor handles the request as an out-of-scope request under SVC-01.
The care supervisor reviews each client's medication assistance log at each supervisory visit (SVC-04) and monthly for clients with regular medication assistance, and corrects any gaps with the aide.
Any aide who violates this policy is retrained, and repeated or serious violations are handled under PER-07.
The Administrator, counsel and the care supervisor review the allowed and forbidden lists at least annually and when the law changes, under GOV-03.

responsibilities.duty: Has the allowed and forbidden lists finalized with counsel, reviews medication incidents and ensures corrective action.
Trains aides, determines whether medication help is permitted for each client, reviews logs and follows up on errors and refusals.
Give only allowed assistance, complete the log each time, report refusals, errors and reactions immediately, and decline forbidden acts.
Manages the client's medications, including filling organizers through the client, family or a licensed provider.

documentation: Medication assistance log
Signed aide acknowledgment of allowed and forbidden acts
Assessment record of the client's medications and self-administration ability
Service plan section on medication assistance
Incident reports on errors, missed doses, refusals and reactions
Records of physician or representative contacts
Annual review of the allowed and forbidden lists

policies.title: Scheduling, Missed Visits and Continuity of Care
policies.applies_to: Scheduler, Administrator, Supervisors and all affiliated home care aides of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure every scheduled visit is staffed by a qualified, registry-cleared aide, that late or missed visits are handled quickly and safely, and that clients receive consistent care from aides who know them.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] assigns only affiliated home care aides who are cleared on the Home Care Aide Registry before direct client contact, have a TB certificate on file, and have completed the 5-hour entry-level training required by HSC §1796.43 and §1796.44. The agency schedules realistic travel time between clients, because travel between clients is paid work time (see PER-10). California has no statutory missed-visit rule for HCOs. As an agency operating standard, the scheduler contacts the client and either sends a replacement aide or notifies the client within 30 minutes of a late or no-show aide, and logs the event. Any client who cannot safely be left alone is escalated immediately. Because the agency is a third-party employer, it cannot rely on the FLSA companionship or live-in exemptions (29 CFR §552.109). Schedules must therefore be built with minimum wage, overtime and paid time rules in mind (see PER-06).

definitions.definition: A scheduled visit that does not start, or that starts more than 30 minutes after the scheduled time, without the client having agreed to the change.
An aide who has not arrived or has not contacted the scheduler by 15 minutes after the scheduled start time. The scheduler begins the 30-minute response clock when the lateness is discovered.

definitions.term: Client who cannot be left alone
definitions.definition: A client whose care plan or intake identifies a need for continuous supervision or hands-on help (for example dementia with wandering, high fall risk, or inability to summon help).
An aide who is registry-listed, has a TB certificate on file, has completed entry-level training, and has no open compliance hold in the personnel file.

procedures: Before building or changing any schedule, the scheduler confirms in the personnel file or scheduling system that the aide is an Eligible Aide: registry listing active, TB certificate on file, and 5-hour entry-level training completed (see PER-01, PER-03, PER-04).

The scheduler does not assign an aide to any client, including a trial or shadow visit, until the Eligible Aide check is complete. If registry status or TB clearance lapses, the scheduler removes the aide from the schedule the same day on notice from the Administrator.
The scheduler matches aides to clients using the service plan (SVC-03): tasks required, language, schedule, dementia status (SVC-11), mobility or transfer needs, and any client or aide preferences.
Each client is assigned a primary aide and, where staffing allows, at least one named backup aide who has been introduced to the client or has reviewed the service plan.
The scheduler builds in realistic travel time between consecutive client visits and records it as paid work time. Mileage and expense rules are handled under PER-10.

The scheduler reviews weekly hours for each aide before publishing the schedule to prevent unplanned overtime and to keep meal and rest breaks achievable (PER-06). Client safety is never sacrificed to avoid overtime. Where overtime is needed, it is paid.

Aides who cannot work a shift notify the scheduler at [PHONE] as soon as they know, and in any case before the shift starts. The scheduler logs the call-off and immediately looks for a qualified replacement.

If an aide is late or has not arrived, the scheduler calls the aide, then calls the client or representative. Within 30 minutes of discovering the lateness, the scheduler must either send a replacement aide or tell the client the expected arrival time or that no replacement is available. The scheduler records every call and its outcome in the Missed Visit Log.

If the client cannot be left alone, the scheduler notifies the on-call Supervisor immediately. The Supervisor secures coverage, which may include another aide, an extended shift by a qualified aide, or contacting the client's representative or emergency contact to arrange interim help.
An aide who is with a client who cannot be left alone does not leave until relief arrives or the Supervisor confirms the client is safe. The extra time is paid and recorded (SVC-07).

If the client or representative cannot be reached and there is reason to believe the client may be unsafe, the Supervisor requests a welfare check through 911 or local law enforcement and follows SVC-08.

If a client reports being neglected, or the missed visit leaves a client without essential care, the Supervisor completes an incident report (SAF-03). If neglect is suspected, the Supervisor follows SAF-01.

For any missed visit that could not be covered, the Supervisor calls the client or representative within one business day, explains what happened, and offers a make-up visit if the client wants one. Billing is adjusted so the client is not charged for care not delivered (CR-06).

Aides who hand off a client to another aide complete a written or electronic handoff note with the client's current status, tasks done, supplies needed, and any concerns. The receiving aide reads it before starting the visit.

The Administrator reviews the Missed Visit Log monthly for patterns by aide, client, time of day and cause. Results go to the QA committee under GOV-04, and the Administrator takes corrective action such as retraining, schedule changes or recruiting.

responsibilities.duty: Verify aide eligibility before every assignment, build schedules with travel time, respond to call-offs and late aides within 30 minutes, and maintain the Missed Visit Log.
Provide on-call coverage decisions, secure coverage for clients who cannot be left alone, call affected clients, and complete incident reports.
Report to scheduled visits on time, notify the scheduler promptly of any absence or delay, stay with a client who cannot be left alone until relieved, and give a handoff note.
Monitor missed-visit trends, ensure staffing levels support the schedule, and report results to QA.

documentation: Weekly schedules and assignment records with aide eligibility check date
Missed Visit Log (client, aide, scheduled time, time discovered, calls made, outcome, replacement aide)
Call-off and on-call records
Handoff notes
Incident reports where applicable
Monthly missed-visit review summary

policies.title: Electronic Visit Verification and Timekeeping (Medi-Cal-funded services; internal timekeeping for all clients)
policies.applies_to: Home care aides, Scheduler, Supervisors, Payroll/Billing staff and Administrator of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To meet federal electronic visit verification (EVV) requirements for Medicaid-funded personal care visits, and to keep accurate contemporaneous time and visit records for every client for payroll, billing and wage-and-hour compliance.
policies.policy: Federal law (42 U.S.C. §1396b(l)) requires EVV for Medicaid-funded personal care services. Before billing any Medi-Cal-funded service, including Community Supports Personal Care and Homemaker Services (PCHS) authorized by a managed care plan (see C28), [AGENCY NAME] confirms with the plan or DHCS the required EVV system, data elements and any deadlines, and follows them. EVV applies only to Medi-Cal-funded visits. For private-pay visits, EVV is not required by the Act. The agency nevertheless requires aides to record actual clock-in, clock-out, location and tasks for every visit, because the agency is a third-party employer that cannot claim the FLSA companionship or live-in exemptions (29 CFR §552.109) and must be able to prove hours worked. Aides record time contemporaneously. Supervisors review exceptions weekly, and every edit requires a documented reason.

definitions.definition: An electronic system that verifies Medicaid-funded personal care visits, as required by the plan or DHCS.
Recording the clock-in or clock-out at the time it occurs, not later from memory or by estimate.
Any visit record that is missing a clock-in or clock-out, is outside the expected location, differs from the schedule beyond the agency's tolerance, or has been manually edited.
A change to a recorded time, location or task entry made by someone other than the aide at the time of the visit.

procedures: Before the agency accepts its first Medi-Cal-funded Community Supports client, the Administrator contacts each managed care plan (and DHCS where needed) in writing to confirm which EVV system must be used, the required data elements, any aggregator or vendor setup, and any deadlines. The answers are filed in the payer file.
The Administrator configures the agency's EVV and timekeeping system to match each payer's requirements and tests it before the first billable visit.
Billing staff do not submit a claim for a Medi-Cal-funded visit unless the visit has a complete EVV record that meets the plan's requirements.

During orientation and before the first shift, each aide is trained on the clock-in and clock-out procedure, the device or app to be used, how to record tasks, and what to do if the system fails. The training is documented in the personnel file (PER-03, PER-05).

Aides clock in on arrival at the client's home and clock out when services end. They record actual times, the location, and the tasks performed for every client, whether Medi-Cal-funded or private-pay.
Aides record travel time between clients as required by PER-10 and meal and rest breaks as required by PER-06, so that all work time is captured.

Aides do not clock in or out for another person, and no one else clocks in or out for an aide. Falsifying time records is grounds for discipline up to termination and is reported to the Administrator (GOV-05).

If the system fails or the aide cannot record at the client's home, the aide calls the scheduler at [PHONE] during the visit, and the scheduler records the call, time and reason in the exception log. The aide enters the actual times in the system when it is available.

Every week, the Supervisor reviews the exception report for missing punches, location mismatches, unusually short or long visits, and manual edits, and follows up with the aide and, where needed, the client.

A manual edit may be made only by a Supervisor or Payroll staff member with edit access. Each edit must include the original entry, the corrected entry, the reason, who made it, who approved it and the date. Aides are told of any change to their time record.
Payroll staff pay aides from the verified time records. Overtime and minimum wage are calculated under PER-06. The agency does not round or auto-deduct time in a way that shortchanges the aide.
Billing staff reconcile client invoices and payer claims to verified visit records before submitting them, and correct any discrepancy before billing (GOV-05, CR-06).
The Administrator reviews a sample of visit records each month against schedules, payroll and invoices, and reports the findings to the QA committee (GOV-04).
Time and visit records are retained as required by RR-01 and PER-05 and are produced on request of a payer or CDSS.

responsibilities.duty: Clock in and out contemporaneously at each visit, record tasks and location, report system failures, and never record time for another person.
Review exceptions weekly, follow up on discrepancies, and approve and document manual edits.
Log system-failure calls and keep schedules aligned with the EVV and timekeeping system.
Pay from verified records, bill only visits with complete verification, and reconcile before submitting claims.
Confirm EVV requirements with each plan or DHCS, maintain the system, and audit records monthly.

documentation: Written EVV requirement confirmations from each plan or DHCS
EVV and timekeeping system records (clock-in, clock-out, location, tasks)
Exception reports and exception log
Manual edit log with reasons and approvals
Aide timekeeping training records
Monthly audit summaries

policies.title: Change in Client Condition and Emergencies in the Home
policies.applies_to: All home care aides, Supervisors, Scheduler and Administrator of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure aides respond correctly to emergencies and report changes in a client's condition promptly, while staying within the non-medical scope of home care services.
policies.policy: Entry-level safety training must cover emergency procedures (HSC §1796.44(b)). Aides call 911 first for any life-threatening emergency and then notify the Supervisor. Aides provide non-medical home care services only (HSC §1796.12) and do not diagnose or treat. They report changes in a client's condition, such as falls, confusion, new pain, skin changes or refused meals, to the Supervisor the same day. The Supervisor notifies the client's representative and the client's physician. If a change suggests abuse or neglect, the agency follows SAF-01 (WIC §15630). If the client's needs now exceed non-medical scope, the agency follows SVC-09 and refers the client to a licensed provider.

definitions.definition: A situation in which a reasonable person would believe the client faces immediate danger to life or health, such as unresponsiveness, difficulty breathing, chest pain, signs of stroke, severe bleeding, a serious fall with injury, choking, or fire.

Any noticeable difference from the client's usual physical, mental, emotional or functional state, including falls, new confusion, new or increased pain, skin changes, changes in eating, drinking or toileting, or a new safety concern in the home.
The person the client has designated, or who is legally authorized, to receive information and make decisions for the client, as recorded in the client record.
Home care services as defined in HSC §1796.12. Aides may not assist with medication that would otherwise require administration or oversight by a licensed health care professional.

procedures: During orientation and before client contact, every aide is trained on emergency procedures, how to call 911, how to give the dispatcher the client's address and condition, and how to reach the Supervisor on the 24-hour line at [PHONE] (PER-03).
In a life-threatening emergency, the aide calls 911 immediately. The aide stays with the client, follows the dispatcher's instructions, and gives only basic first aid within the aide's training.
As soon as it is safe, the aide calls the Supervisor at [PHONE]. If the aide cannot reach the Supervisor, the aide leaves a message and tries the Administrator at [PHONE].

The aide gives emergency responders the client's emergency information sheet, medication list and advance directive information if they are in the home, but does not make treatment decisions for the client.

The Supervisor notifies the client's representative as soon as possible and records the time and who was notified. If the client is taken to the hospital, the Supervisor arranges for the aide to send along any needed information and follows up on the client's status.

For non-emergency changes in condition, the aide reports the change to the Supervisor the same day. The aide describes what was seen or heard, when it started, and what the client said, using facts rather than diagnoses.

The aide does not diagnose, give medical advice, change or stop a medication, or treat the condition. If the client asks the aide to do a task that would require licensed medical oversight, the aide declines and reports the request (SVC-01, SVC-05).

The Supervisor reviews the report the same day, contacts the client or representative, and notifies the client's physician or recommends that the client contact the physician. The Supervisor records who was contacted, when, and the response.
If the change signals a possible need for a different level of care, the Supervisor conducts or arranges a reassessment (SVC-02) and updates the service plan (SVC-03).

If the change or the circumstances suggest physical abuse, neglect, abandonment, isolation or financial abuse, the aide and Supervisor follow SAF-01 without delay, and each mandated reporter makes the report required by WIC §15630.
If the client's needs now exceed what a non-medical home care agency may provide, the Supervisor tells the client and representative, helps with referrals to a licensed provider, and follows SVC-09.
The aide completes an incident report (SAF-03) the same day for any emergency call, fall, injury, or significant change in condition, and the Supervisor reviews and signs it.
The Supervisor makes a follow-up call or visit within [NUMBER OF DAYS] days of any emergency or significant change, and records the client's status.
The Administrator reviews emergency and condition-change events monthly for trends and training needs and reports to the QA committee (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Call 911 for life-threatening emergencies, report changes in condition to the Supervisor the same day, stay within non-medical scope, and complete incident reports.
Be reachable 24 hours, notify the client's representative and physician, reassess needs, ensure mandated reports are made, and follow up.
Ensure staff are trained on emergency procedures, review trends, and ensure referrals and discontinuation follow SVC-09.

documentation: Incident reports (SAF-03)
Supervisor notification log (who, when, what was reported)

policies.title: Discharge, Transfer and Discontinuation of Services
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Supervisors, Scheduler, billing staff and aides of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure services end in an orderly, documented and safe manner, with fair notice, help finding other providers, and no abandonment of clients with unmet safety needs.
policies.policy: The Home Care Services Consumer Protection Act has no discharge-notice rule for HCOs, so the terms for ending services are set in the client's service agreement (see CR-06). As an agency operating standard, [AGENCY NAME] gives written notice stating the reasons and listing referrals to other providers, at least 14 days before ending services where it is safe to do so. The agency may discontinue services immediately for threats to the safety of aides, non-payment after notice, or client needs that go beyond non-medical home care services as defined in HSC §1796.12. The agency does not abandon a client with unmet safety needs. Where a client is at risk, the agency notifies the client's representative and, if warranted, follows SAF-01 for any report to Adult Protective Services. The agency documents a discharge summary and closes the record under RR-01.

definitions.definition: Ending all home care services to a client, whether at the client's request, by agreement, or by the agency.
Moving a client's care to another provider or to a different level of care, with the client's agreement.
Ending services without the 14-day notice because of a safety threat to aides, non-payment after notice, or needs beyond non-medical scope.
A client who, if services stop, would be without needed help and could be harmed, for example because of cognitive impairment, inability to get food or medication, or lack of a caregiver.

procedures: Only the Administrator may approve an agency-initiated discharge. The Supervisor submits a written recommendation with the reason and supporting documentation.

If the client or representative asks to end services, the Supervisor records the request, the date and the requested end date, asks about the reason, and confirms the request in writing or by a documented call.

Before issuing a notice, the Supervisor confirms that the service agreement terms (CR-06) are being followed and reviews whether the problem can be resolved, for example through a service plan change (SVC-03), a different aide, or a payment arrangement.

For a planned discontinuation, the Administrator sends written notice to the client and representative at least 14 days before the end date where safe. The notice states the reasons, the last day of service, and a list of referrals to other providers, and gives contact information at [PHONE] for questions.
The agency continues to provide services through the notice period unless an immediate discontinuation condition applies.

Immediate discontinuation is permitted only for threats to the safety of aides, non-payment after written notice, or needs beyond non-medical scope. The Administrator documents the facts and the reason before acting and gives the client and representative written notice the same day or as soon as possible.

If needs exceed non-medical scope, the Supervisor helps the client and representative arrange a referral to a licensed provider, such as a home health agency or the client's physician, and arranges for a safe transition of care where possible.

Before the final visit, the Supervisor confirms that the client has a safe plan: who will provide help, how the client will get meals and medications, and who to call. The Supervisor does not end services in a way that leaves a client with unmet safety needs.

If the client is at risk and no safe plan exists, the Supervisor notifies the representative and any emergency contact. If abuse or neglect is suspected, the Supervisor follows SAF-01 for the report to Adult Protective Services or local law enforcement.

If the client is moving to another provider, the Supervisor, with the client's written authorization, gives the new provider the relevant information (CR-03). The agency shares only what is authorized or permitted by law.
Where the client is covered by a Medi-Cal managed care plan or other payer, the Supervisor notifies the plan or payer as the contract requires (SVC-10).
The Scheduler removes the client from future schedules after the last day and informs the aides assigned to the client.
Billing staff issue a final invoice, apply any credit or refund owed under the service agreement, and send it with a final accounting within the time stated in the agreement (CR-06).
The Supervisor ensures return of the client's property and any agency items and records the return (CR-04).

The Supervisor completes a discharge summary covering the reason, date, services provided, condition at discharge, referrals given, notices sent, and who was notified. The Administrator signs it, and the record is closed and retained under RR-01.
The Administrator reviews discharges quarterly for patterns and any grievance related to discontinuation (CR-02, GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Approve agency-initiated discharges, issue notices, and review discharge trends.
Recommend discharge with documentation, ensure a safe transition plan, make referrals, notify representatives and payers, and complete the discharge summary.
Remove the client from the schedule and inform assigned aides.
Issue the final invoice and any refund or credit under the service agreement.

Written notice to client and representative with referral list

policies.title: Coordination with Medi-Cal Managed Care Plans (Community Supports), IHSS and Other Payers
policies.applies_to: Administrator, intake staff, Supervisors and billing staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure the agency understands the differences among IHSS, Medi-Cal Community Supports, the HCBA Waiver and private payment, follows each payer's rules, and coordinates care so that clients do not receive duplicate or conflicting services.
policies.policy: In-Home Supportive Services (IHSS) pays individual providers chosen by the consumer through state payroll, not agencies, and IHSS providers are not home care organizations (HSC §1796.17). A contract mode exists only in San Francisco. Medi-Cal Community Supports Personal Care and Homemaker Services (PCHS) are authorized and paid by each managed care plan under its contract with the agency. The agency follows the plan's authorization, rate and claims rules. The DHCS pricing benchmark is non-binding and does not set the agency's rate. Medi-Cal Personal Care Agencies serving the HCBA Waiver are exempt from HCO licensure, but an HCO that is not enrolled for the waiver is not covered by that exemption. Medi-Cal provider enrollment (PAVE) is pursued only if a plan requires it. The agency coordinates with IHSS or the plan when a client receives other hours. Medicaid-funded personal care visits are subject to EVV (SVC-07).

definitions.definition: In-Home Supportive Services, a county-administered, consumer-directed program that pays individual providers through state payroll.
A plan-offered Medi-Cal managed care benefit for Personal Care and Homemaker Services. IHSS is the primary program, and eligibility and provider requirements are set by DHCS policy and each plan.
The Home and Community-Based Alternatives Waiver, which offers waiver personal care services. Medi-Cal Personal Care Agencies serving it are exempt from HCO licensure.
The Provider Application and Validation for Enrollment portal for Medi-Cal provider enrollment.
The plan's written approval of the type, amount and duration of services for a named client.

procedures: At intake (SVC-02), intake staff ask each prospective client about all sources of coverage and help: IHSS, Medi-Cal managed care plan, HCBA Waiver, long-term care insurance, Veterans benefits, other agencies, and private pay. The answers are recorded in the client record.

Intake staff explain to the client that the agency does not provide IHSS and that IHSS providers are individuals paid through state payroll. If the client is eligible for IHSS and wants IHSS services, intake staff refer the client to the county IHSS office and do not suggest that the agency can serve as an IHSS provider (except where a county contract mode applies).

Before accepting a Community Supports client, the Administrator confirms the agency has a current contract with that managed care plan and that the plan has authorized the services. The agency does not start billable services without a written authorization on file.

The Administrator keeps a payer file for each plan with the contract, provider manual, rate sheet, authorization process, claims rules, contact names, and EVV requirements (SVC-07). The file is reviewed at least yearly.

The agency follows each plan's authorization, rate, documentation and claims rules. The DHCS pricing benchmark is used only as a reference in negotiation and is not treated as a binding or published rate.

The agency provides only the services authorized and in the amounts authorized. If a client needs more or different services, the Supervisor asks the plan for a new authorization before providing them, or offers the extra hours as private pay under a service agreement (CR-06), with the client's informed written agreement.

The Administrator does not represent the agency as exempt from HCO licensure. The HCBA Waiver Personal Care Agency exemption applies only to Medi-Cal Personal Care Agencies serving the waiver, and this agency is licensed as an HCO.

The Administrator checks the requirements of each plan to find out whether Medi-Cal provider enrollment (PAVE) is needed. If a plan requires PAVE, the Administrator completes enrollment before billing that plan and files the confirmation.

When a client also receives IHSS hours, Medi-Cal services or other paid help, the Supervisor, with the client's authorization (CR-03), coordinates with the IHSS social worker or plan care manager to avoid overlap, so that the same hours or tasks are not billed to or provided by two sources.

The Supervisor sends the plan or care manager updates on changes in condition, hospitalizations, missed visits and discharge as the contract requires (SVC-08, SVC-09), and shares only the minimum necessary information.

Billing staff submit claims only for services authorized and delivered, supported by verified visit records, and in the format the plan requires. Denials and underpayments are reviewed and corrected within the plan's time limits (GOV-05).

Billing staff never bill a client or representative for amounts a plan has denied or covered unless the client agreed in writing in advance to private payment for that service, and the Administrator reviews every such case.

Each year, the Administrator reviews the DHCS Community Supports policy guide, plan notices and any changes to IHSS or the HCBA Waiver, updates this policy and related procedures, and trains intake and billing staff (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Maintain plan contracts and payer files, confirm authorizations and any PAVE requirement, and monitor program changes.
Identify all payers at intake, explain IHSS accurately, and refer clients to the county IHSS office when appropriate.
Coordinate with IHSS and plan care managers, ensure only authorized services are provided, and request new authorizations.
Bill only authorized and verified services, follow plan claims rules, and resolve denials.

Plan contracts, rate sheets and payer files

Coordination notes with IHSS social workers and plan care managers

policies.title: Dementia Care Practices and Training Readiness (effective 1/1/2027)
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Supervisors, Scheduler, trainers and all affiliated home care aides of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To prepare the agency for the dementia training requirement that takes effect on 1/1/2027, and to ensure clients with dementia are safely served by aides trained in their special care needs.
policies.policy: From 1/1/2027, annual aide training must include the special care needs of clients with dementia (HSC §1796.44(c)(6), SB 412, Stats. 2025, ch. 414). The 5-hour annual minimum is unchanged, and the 5-hour entry-level requirement (2 hours orientation and 3 hours safety) is unchanged. The SB 412 bill digest also refers to dementia training before providing home care, while the chaptered text lists it only under annual training. Counsel should confirm whether a pre-service dementia component is required. Until that is confirmed, [AGENCY NAME] follows the conservative approach: dementia content is included in the 3-hour entry safety block or in the first annual module, for any aide assigned to a client with dementia, before that aide is assigned. The agency documents dementia status at intake, assigns trained aides, and uses a safety plan for wandering, refusal of care and sundowning.

definitions.definition: A condition causing a decline in memory, thinking, judgment or communication that interferes with daily life, including Alzheimer's disease and related disorders, as diagnosed by a physician or as reported by the client's representative or physician.
Leaving the home or safe area without awareness of danger or without being able to return safely.
Increased confusion, agitation or restlessness in late afternoon or evening.
Training content covering the special care needs of clients with dementia, delivered in person or online (HSC §1796.44(d)).

procedures: By [DATE BEFORE 1/1/2027], the Administrator designs or selects a dementia training module covering the special care needs of clients with dementia, including communication, behavior changes, safety (wandering, falls, kitchen and home hazards), personal care with a client who resists, nutrition and hydration, caregiver stress, and abuse and neglect warning signs. The module is added to the training plan (PER-03) with trainer, objectives and a sample log.

Starting 1/1/2027, the Administrator includes the dementia module as part of each aide's 5-hour annual training. It does not add to or replace the other required annual topics, and the total remains at least 5 hours.

The Administrator consults counsel before 1/1/2027 about whether dementia training is required before an aide first provides care, and records the answer in the policy file. If counsel confirms a pre-service requirement, the agency applies it to all new aides.

Until that confirmation, the agency applies the conservative approach: dementia content is built into the 3-hour entry safety block or delivered as the aide's first annual module, and an aide is not assigned to a client with dementia until that content is complete.

At intake and assessment (SVC-02), the Supervisor asks whether the client has a diagnosis of dementia or symptoms such as memory loss, wandering, confusion or agitation. The answer, its source and the date are recorded in the client record. Without a diagnosis, the Supervisor documents observed signs and refers the client to the physician.

The Supervisor completes a dementia safety plan for each client with dementia, covering wandering risk and exit precautions, refusal of care, sundowning, home hazards, medication reminders only within the limits of SVC-05, emergency contacts, and what the aide does when the client is missing.
The safety plan is written into the service plan (SVC-03). The Supervisor reviews it with the assigned aide before the first visit and reviews it with the client's representative at each plan update.

The Scheduler checks the training record before assigning an aide to a client with dementia and assigns only aides who have completed the dementia content. If no trained aide is available, the Scheduler tells the Supervisor, and the service start is delayed or the client is referred.
The Scheduler gives a client with dementia a consistent primary aide and a trained backup aide whenever possible, to reduce confusion (SVC-06).

If a client with dementia is missing or leaves the home, the aide calls 911 immediately, then the Supervisor, and follows the safety plan and SVC-08. The Supervisor notifies the client's representative and completes an incident report (SAF-03).

If a client with dementia refuses care, the aide does not force care. The aide uses the techniques in the safety plan, ensures the client is safe, and reports the refusal to the Supervisor the same day. The Supervisor decides whether to adjust the plan.
Aides who observe signs of abuse, neglect or exploitation of a client with dementia, who may be unable to report it, follow SAF-01 immediately.

The Administrator tracks completion by aide in the training log and reports quarterly to the QA committee on dementia training completion, the number of dementia clients and any related incidents (GOV-04).
The Administrator reviews this policy within 90 days after 1/1/2027, and again when counsel or CDSS provides further guidance on SB 412, and updates it under GOV-03.

responsibilities.duty: Build the dementia module into the training plan, obtain counsel's confirmation, track completion, and report to QA.
Document dementia status at intake, write the dementia safety plan, brief aides, and review incidents.
Assign only aides who have completed the dementia content to clients with dementia.
Complete dementia training, follow the safety plan, and report wandering, refusal of care and other concerns promptly.

Training logs showing dementia content completion by aide and date
Counsel's confirmation on pre-service requirement

Incident reports (SAF-03)
