policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting (Elder and Dependent Adults)
policies.applies_to: All affiliated home care aides, supervisors, schedulers, office staff, the Administrator and any volunteer who has contact with clients
policies.purpose: To protect clients who are elders or dependent adults from abuse, neglect and exploitation, and to make sure every suspected incident is reported to the right agency within the time California law requires. This policy also explains how [AGENCY NAME] keeps the reports CDSS may review.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has zero tolerance for abuse, neglect, abandonment, isolation, abduction or financial exploitation of any client. Every person with full or intermittent responsibility for the care of an elder or dependent adult is a mandated reporter under WIC §15630(a), whether or not paid. This includes every aide and every staff member who cares for or supervises care for a client. Each mandated reporter has an individual legal duty to report observed, known or reasonably suspected physical abuse, abandonment, abduction, isolation, financial abuse or neglect. This includes abuse the client discloses (WIC §15630(b)(1)). The report is made by telephone or the confidential internet tool immediately or as soon as practicably possible. A written or internet report follows within 2 working days. For abuse in a client's home, the report goes to the county adult protective services (APS) agency or local law enforcement (WIC §15630(b)(1)(F)). [AGENCY NAME] will never require supervisor or Administrator approval before a report is made, will never screen or delay a report, and will never retaliate against anyone who reports in good faith. The agency keeps a copy of each suspected-abuse report and makes it available to CDSS during normal business hours (HSC §1796.42(e)). A CDSS cross-report to law enforcement and APS does not replace the agency's own report (HSC §1796.52(e)).

definitions.definition: A client aged 65 or older.
A client aged 18 to 64 whose physical or mental limitations restrict the ability to carry out normal activities or to protect his or her rights.
A person with full or intermittent responsibility for the care or custody of an elder or dependent adult, paid or unpaid, who must report abuse under WIC §15630.
An objectively reasonable belief, based on facts a person in the same position would believe, that abuse or neglect may have occurred. Proof is not required.
Physical abuse, abandonment, abduction, isolation, financial abuse and neglect, as listed in WIC §15630(b)(1).
The county Adult Protective Services agency that receives reports of abuse of elders and dependent adults living in their own homes.
Any day other than a Saturday, Sunday or state holiday.

procedures: The Administrator will look up the APS hotline number and the local law enforcement non-emergency number for every county [AGENCY NAME] serves. These numbers will be recorded as [COUNTY APS PHONE] and [LOCAL LAW ENFORCEMENT NON-EMERGENCY NUMBER]. The Administrator will post them in the office, print them in the aide handbook and put them on a wallet card given to each aide at orientation. The Administrator will re-verify the numbers at least annually and whenever a new county is added.

At orientation, before the aide is alone with any client, each aide and staff member receives this policy and signs a statement acknowledging that they are a mandated reporter with an individual duty to report. The signed statement goes in the personnel record (PER-05).
If a client is in immediate danger or needs emergency medical care, the aide or staff member calls 911 first, then follows the steps below.

Any aide or staff member who observes, learns of or reasonably suspects abuse, neglect or exploitation, or hears a client disclose it, must make a telephone or confidential internet report to APS or local law enforcement immediately or as soon as practicably possible. The aide does not wait for a supervisor, does not investigate and does not confront the suspected abuser.

When making the report, the reporter gives their name and contact information, the client's name and address, the nature and location of the suspected abuse, the date it occurred or was discovered, the suspected person if known, and any injuries seen. The reporter writes down the name of the person who took the report, the date, the time and any report or reference number.

After the telephone or internet report, the reporter notifies the supervisor on call at [PHONE] so the agency can protect the client and plan next steps. This notice is informational only. It is not an approval step, and it must not delay or replace the reporter's own report.

The reporter submits the written or internet follow-up report within 2 working days of the telephone report, using the form or confidential internet tool designated by APS or law enforcement. Office staff will help the reporter complete the report on request, but the reporter signs and submits it.

The reporter gives a copy of the written report, with the telephone log details, to the Administrator within 1 working day of submitting it. The Administrator keeps the copy in a separate, confidential abuse-report file that is not part of the client's routine service record. The file is organized so any report can be produced to CDSS during normal business hours (HSC §1796.42(e)).

If the suspected abuser is an aide or other staff member, the Administrator immediately removes that person from contact with the client pending the outcome. The Administrator then arranges a safe replacement for the client and preserves schedules, timesheets and notes. The agency does not conduct an interview that could interfere with the APS or law enforcement inquiry unless those agencies agree to it.

If an aide is separated because of abuse, neglect or exploitation, the Administrator also follows PER-11 and notifies CDSS immediately that the individual is no longer employed as an affiliated home care aide (HSC §1796.43(a)(3)).

The Administrator notifies the client's legal representative or emergency contact of the report unless doing so could place the client at risk or the investigating agency has asked the agency not to. The Administrator documents the decision and the reason.

The Administrator cooperates fully with APS, law enforcement and CDSS. CDSS cross-reports abuse reports it receives to law enforcement and APS and has no duty to investigate beyond that. [AGENCY NAME] therefore never treats a CDSS notice as having satisfied its own reporting duty (HSC §1796.52(e)).

No person may be disciplined, threatened, or have hours, assignments or pay reduced for making a report in good faith. A supervisor who discourages, delays, edits or screens a report is subject to discipline up to termination. Any employee who believes this has happened may report it directly to the Administrator or to [PHONE].

Prevention measures: the agency completes background clearance and registry screening before client contact (PER-02), supervises aides under SVC-04, follows the financial protections in CR-04 and applies the boundaries in PER-07. Supervisors watch for warning signs during supervisory visits and client calls, such as unexplained injuries, fear of a caregiver, missing money or property, poor hygiene, weight loss or isolation.
Annual training for every aide must include how to report, prevent and detect abuse and neglect (HSC §1796.44(c)). The training is documented in the personnel record (PER-03, PER-05).

The Administrator reviews every abuse report, with identifying details protected, at least quarterly. The review looks for patterns by client, aide, shift or referral source, and results go to the quality program (GOV-04).
The Administrator reviews the abuse-report file at least annually to make sure every report has a complete copy, that reports are retrievable on request and that retention follows RR-01.

responsibilities.duty: Report observed, known or reasonably suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, and abuse a client discloses. Submit the written follow-up within 2 working days. Give a copy to the Administrator. Never investigate or confront.

Post and verify APS and law enforcement numbers, protect clients, remove staff under suspicion, keep the abuse-report file available to CDSS, ensure training occurs and prevent retaliation or screening of reports.
Support the reporter, assist with forms on request, protect the client, notify the Administrator and never require approval before a report.
Arrange replacement coverage when an aide is removed and preserve schedule and time records.

documentation: Signed mandated-reporter acknowledgment for each aide and staff member
Copy of each telephone log and written or internet report in the abuse-report file
Date and time of report, agency contacted and report or reference number
Notes on notification of the representative or emergency contact and any decision to delay it
Records of steps taken to protect the client, including aide removal and replacement
Training records showing annual abuse reporting, prevention and detection content
Quarterly review notes and annual file audit

policies.title: Reporting Suspected Child Abuse in the Home
policies.applies_to: All affiliated home care aides, supervisors, schedulers, office staff, the Administrator and any volunteer
policies.purpose: To make sure that any suspected or known child abuse observed by [AGENCY NAME] staff in a client's home is reported as California law requires, and that a copy of each report is kept for CDSS review.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] reports suspected or known child abuse as required by Penal Code §§11164 to 11174.3 (HSC §1796.42(e)). Staff must report whenever, in the course of work, they know of or reasonably suspect that a child is being abused or neglected, including a child who lives in or visits a client's home. The Administrator keeps a copy of each report available to CDSS for review during normal business hours (HSC §1796.42(e)). No one needs supervisor approval to report, and no one will be retaliated against for reporting in good faith. The specific timeframes, receiving agencies and forms in the Penal Code sections cited above are maintained by the Administrator in the current reporting packet described below, which is reviewed by counsel and updated through GOV-03 whenever the law changes. In every case the telephone report is made immediately or as soon as practicably possible, as an operator standard, and the written report follows within the time set by the Penal Code sections cited above.

definitions.definition: A person under 18 years of age.
An objectively reasonable belief, based on facts a person in the same position would believe, that abuse or neglect may have occurred. Proof is not required.

The Administrator's current set of child-abuse reporting instructions: county child welfare or child protective services telephone number [COUNTY CPS HOTLINE], local law enforcement non-emergency number [LOCAL LAW ENFORCEMENT NON-EMERGENCY NUMBER], the current written report form and the current written-report deadline as confirmed by counsel.

procedures: Before publication of this manual, the Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) has counsel confirm the telephone deadline, written-report deadline, receiving agencies and current form required under Penal Code §§11164 to 11174.3. Counsel's confirmation is placed in the reporting packet and the packet is dated.

The Administrator places the reporting packet in the office, makes it available to on-call supervisors and puts the county child welfare and law enforcement numbers in the aide handbook and on each aide's wallet card.

At orientation, each aide and staff member receives this policy and the packet and signs an acknowledgment that they understand the duty to report. The acknowledgment goes in the personnel record (PER-05).
If a child is in immediate danger or needs urgent medical care, the aide or staff member calls 911 first.

An aide or staff member who sees, learns of or reasonably suspects child abuse or neglect makes a telephone report to the agency named in the reporting packet immediately or as soon as practicably possible. The reporter does not wait for a supervisor, does not investigate, does not question the child beyond what is needed to keep the child safe and does not confront the family.

The reporter gives the child's name and location, the reporter's own name and contact details, the facts observed or heard and the suspected person if known. The reporter records the name of the person who took the report, the date, the time and any reference number.

The reporter completes and submits the written report on the current form within the deadline stated in the reporting packet. Office staff will help with the form on request, but the reporter signs and submits it.

The reporter gives the Administrator a copy of the written report and telephone details within 1 working day of submission. The Administrator files it with the agency's suspected-abuse reports so it can be produced to CDSS on request (HSC §1796.42(e)). Child-abuse reports are kept confidential and are not placed in the routine client service record.

The reporter informs the on-call supervisor at [PHONE] after the telephone report so the agency can support the aide and review the client's service plan. This is notice only and not an approval step.

The Administrator does not tell the client or the family that a report was made if doing so could endanger the child or interfere with the investigation. The Administrator follows the instructions of the receiving agency.

If the suspected person is an aide or staff member, the Administrator immediately removes that person from contact with the client household pending the outcome and follows SAF-01 and PER-11, including immediate notice to CDSS if the person is no longer employed as an affiliated home care aide (HSC §1796.43(a)(3)).
If a client is also suspected to be a victim or perpetrator involving an adult, the reporter also follows SAF-01 for elder and dependent adult reporting. A single event can require both reports.
Annual training covers how to report, prevent and detect abuse and neglect (HSC §1796.44(c)). The Administrator records completion in the personnel record (PER-03, PER-05).
The Administrator reviews the reporting packet at least annually and whenever the law changes. The review is recorded under GOV-03.

responsibilities.duty: Report suspected or known child abuse by telephone immediately or as soon as practicably possible, submit the written report on time and give a copy to the Administrator.
Maintain the reporting packet with counsel, keep copies of every report available to CDSS, remove staff under suspicion and prevent retaliation or screening.
Support the reporter and never require approval before a report is made.

documentation: Signed acknowledgment of the child-abuse reporting duty for each employee
Copy of each child-abuse report and telephone details, filed with the agency's suspected-abuse reports
Reporting packet with counsel's confirmation date and review dates
Training records showing abuse reporting content
Notes on any aide removal or replacement

policies.title: Incident Reporting
policies.applies_to: All affiliated home care aides, supervisors, schedulers, office staff and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To make sure every incident involving a client, aide or the agency is reported internally, documented, reviewed and acted on, so that clients are protected and patterns are identified.
policies.policy: The Home Care Services Consumer Protection Act does not set a general incident-report requirement for Home Care Organizations. The only statutory reports in this program are suspected-abuse reports (HSC §1796.42(e)) and the notice to CDSS when an aide is no longer employed (HSC §1796.43(a)(3)). The internal incident reporting system described here is an operator-adopted standard that goes beyond those requirements. Under this standard, every aide must tell the supervisor immediately about a reportable incident and complete a written incident report within 24 hours. Supervisors notify the client's representative and review incidents for trends. Incident reporting never replaces or delays a required abuse report, which must be made under SAF-01 or SAF-02 regardless of this policy. Aide injuries also follow PER-12.

definitions.definition: A fall, injury, hospitalization, property loss or damage, medication event, client death, aide injury, allegation against staff, or aide or vehicle accident, or any other event that affects client safety or the agency.
A missed, refused, doubled or wrong-time medication, or any problem with medication reminders or assistance with self-administration (see SVC-05).
Any complaint or statement that an aide or staff member harmed, neglected, stole from, mistreated or acted improperly toward a client.
The agency's written form recording who, what, when, where, how, what was done and who was notified.

procedures: If anyone is hurt or in danger, the aide first calls 911 and gives emergency assistance within the aide's scope of work (SVC-08). Reporting steps follow after the emergency is addressed.
The aide notifies the supervisor on call at [PHONE] immediately after any reportable incident, by telephone and not by text alone.

The aide completes a written incident report within 24 hours of the incident, stating facts only: date, time, location, people involved, what happened, what the aide observed, actions taken and who was notified. Opinions and blame are not recorded.

The supervisor reviews the report within 1 business day, confirms the client is safe and decides what immediate follow-up is needed, such as a visit, call to the client's physician at the representative's request, or a change in the schedule.

If an incident involves suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation of an elder or dependent adult, the person who becomes aware of it reports it under SAF-01. If it involves a child, the person reports under SAF-02. The incident report is completed in addition to, not instead of, those reports.

For a client death, the aide calls 911 unless a valid, documented end-of-life directive applies and the representative has given other instructions. The supervisor then notifies the client's representative and emergency contacts and the Administrator. The Administrator documents the event and closes the service agreement under SVC-09.

For an aide injury or illness caused by work, the supervisor makes sure the aide gets care and then follows PER-12 so the workers' compensation claim is handled under the policy the agency must maintain (HSC §1796.42(b)).
For an aide or vehicle accident, the aide reports it to the supervisor immediately, and the Administrator reviews it under SAF-07 and PER-10.
For property loss, damage or alleged theft, the supervisor follows CR-04 and records the client's report and the aide's account separately.

For any allegation against staff, the supervisor notifies the Administrator the same day. The Administrator decides whether to remove the aide from the client pending review and documents the decision. If the allegation is of abuse, SAF-01 applies.
The supervisor notifies the client's representative of any significant incident the same day, unless the representative cannot be reached. In that case the supervisor documents each attempt.
If an incident leads to an aide no longer being employed, the Administrator follows PER-11 and notifies CDSS immediately (HSC §1796.43(a)(3)).
The Administrator signs each incident report as reviewed within 5 business days and records any corrective action, such as retraining, a service plan update (SVC-03) or a change in aide assignment.
The Administrator summarizes incidents monthly by type, aide, client and time of day, looking for trends. The summary goes to the quality program (GOV-04).

Incident reports are filed in a confidential incident log and referenced, but not copied in full, in the client record (RR-01). Reports related to abuse are kept in the separate abuse-report file under SAF-01.
Staff may not alter an incident report after it is signed. Corrections are made by dated addendum.

responsibilities.duty: Get help in an emergency, notify the supervisor immediately, complete the written report within 24 hours and stick to facts.
Confirm client safety, notify the representative, review the report within 1 business day and escalate allegations and abuse concerns.
Sign off on every report, direct corrective action, maintain the incident log, review trends monthly and make required notices to CDSS.

documentation: Incident report form for each event, with addenda
Incident log with dates and review sign-off
Notification record to the client's representative with each attempt
Corrective action notes
Monthly incident summary and trend review
Workers' compensation claim reference where an aide is injured (PER-12)

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All affiliated home care aides, supervisors and office staff who have client contact
policies.purpose: To reduce the risk of spreading infection to clients and staff, to meet the entry-level infection control training and TB examination requirements of the Act, and to protect employees from bloodborne pathogen exposure.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires every aide to complete entry-level safety training, which includes infection control, before being present with a client (HSC §1796.44(b)). Every aide must have a tuberculosis examination under HSC §1796.45 as a condition of initial and continuing employment. Aides do not work while they have a contagious illness. The OSHA bloodborne pathogens standard (29 CFR 1910.1030) applies to employees with occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious material. Where it applies, the agency provides gloves and personal protective equipment, a hand hygiene protocol, a sharps and soiled-linen protocol, an exposure incident procedure and an offer of hepatitis B vaccine. Other Cal/OSHA standards that may apply to the agency have not been confirmed. The Administrator will confirm them with counsel and update this policy through GOV-03.

definitions.definition: Basic infection control practices used with every client: hand hygiene, gloves and other protective equipment when contact with body fluids is likely, safe handling of sharps and soiled linen, and cleaning of surfaces.
Personal protective equipment such as gloves, masks, gowns and eye protection.
A specific contact of eye, mouth, other mucous membrane, non-intact skin or skin puncture with blood or other potentially infectious material while working.
A CDC-recommended, FDA-licensed test for tuberculosis infection. If positive, it is followed by a chest X-ray.
Reasonably anticipated contact with blood or other potentially infectious material while performing job duties.

procedures: Before any client contact, each aide completes the entry-level safety training required by HSC §1796.44(b), which includes infection control. The training is documented in the personnel record (PER-03, PER-05).

Each aide must have a TB examination 90 days before employment or within 7 days after hire, as HSC §1796.45(a) requires. The exam is a CDC-recommended, FDA-licensed TB infection test and, if positive, a chest X-ray. The aide submits the practitioner's certificate after each exam and the agency keeps it on file (PER-04).

An aide with a positive TB test may not work unless the agency has documentation from a licensed medical professional that the aide poses no risk of spreading disease (HSC §1796.45(b)). The Administrator confirms and files this documentation before the aide is scheduled.

The agency repeats the TB exam at least every 2 years for aides whose results are negative. Once a positive test has been followed by an X-ray, repeat exams are no longer required (HSC §1796.45(c)). The Administrator tracks each aide's due date and schedules reminders 60 days ahead.

For an aide transferring from another HCO, the Administrator accepts a certificate from within the past 2 years, or written verification from the prior HCO that it holds the certificate with a copy provided, before the aide starts (HSC §1796.45(f)).

Aides practice hand hygiene before and after client contact, before preparing food, after toileting assistance, after removing gloves and after handling soiled items. Aides carry hand sanitizer and use soap and water when hands are visibly soiled.

The agency supplies gloves in all required sizes and other PPE at no cost to aides. Aides wear gloves for any contact with blood, body fluids, broken skin, wound drainage or soiled items and change gloves between tasks and between clients.

Aides do not handle sharps beyond the scope in SVC-01. If a client's used sharps are found, aides do not recap, bend or pick them up by hand. They tell the client or representative and, if unavoidable, use a tool such as tongs and place the item in a puncture-resistant container.

Aides handle soiled linen and clothing with gloves, bag it at the point of use without shaking it and wash it in the hottest water the fabric allows. Contaminated surfaces are cleaned with a household disinfectant following label directions.

Aides who may have occupational exposure are offered the hepatitis B vaccine at no cost, as 29 CFR 1910.1030 requires. An aide who declines signs a declination, which is kept in the personnel record and may be revoked at any time.

After an exposure incident, the aide washes the site with soap and water or flushes mucous membranes immediately, then notifies the supervisor at [PHONE] right away. The supervisor makes sure the aide receives a confidential medical evaluation and follow-up promptly. The Administrator completes an exposure incident record and follows PER-12 and SAF-03.

Aides do not work while they have fever, vomiting, diarrhea, an infectious rash, active respiratory infection or other contagious illness. The aide calls the scheduler as early as possible so coverage can be arranged (SVC-06). Aides may not be penalized for staying home when contagious, and sick leave is handled under PER-09.

Supervisors screen for infection concerns when scheduling. If a client has a reportable or contagious illness, the supervisor tells aides what precautions to take, respecting the client's privacy (CR-03).
Aides who notice signs of infection in a client, such as fever, wound redness or drainage, cough or new confusion, report them under SVC-08.

The Administrator reviews infection prevention practices, supply levels and exposure incidents at least annually and records the review through the quality program (GOV-04). The Administrator will confirm with counsel which additional Cal/OSHA standards apply to the agency and update this policy through GOV-03.

responsibilities.duty: Complete training, complete TB exams on time, use standard precautions and PPE, stay home when contagious and report exposures immediately.
Reinforce practices at supervisory visits, supply PPE, manage exposure incidents and coordinate coverage when an aide is ill.
Track TB exam due dates, hold all certificates, offer hepatitis B vaccine, maintain exposure records and review this policy at least annually.

documentation: Entry-level safety and infection control training record
TB practitioner certificates for each aide and a tracking log with due dates
Licensed medical professional documentation for any aide with a positive TB test
Hepatitis B vaccine offer, acceptance or declination form
Exposure incident records and medical evaluation referral notes
PPE supply log
Annual infection control review notes

policies.title: Client Emergency and Disaster Plans
policies.applies_to: All affiliated home care aides, supervisors, schedulers, office staff and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To prepare each client and the agency for medical emergencies and for disasters such as wildfire, earthquake, power shutoff and extreme heat, and to keep aides and clients as safe as reasonably possible.
policies.policy: Entry-level safety training must cover emergency procedures before an aide is present with a client (HSC §1796.44(b)). The Act does not contain a specific disaster-plan rule for Home Care Organizations, so the disaster planning in this policy is an operator-adopted standard. At intake, [AGENCY NAME] rates each client's disaster risk and records emergency contacts and evacuation help. The agency maintains a prioritized call list for use in wildfire, earthquake, power shutoff and heat events, an after-hours coordinator line and a backup staffing plan. [AGENCY NAME] does not provide medical or rescue services. Aides call 911 in life-threatening emergencies and help clients within the scope in SVC-01.

definitions.definition: The agency's assessment of how much help a client would need in an emergency, based on oxygen or powered equipment, mobility limits, cognitive impairment, living alone and similar factors.
A list of clients ranked by risk rating, used to decide who is contacted first during a disaster.
The staff member answering the agency's emergency line at [PHONE] outside normal business hours.
A planned or unplanned utility outage that can affect oxygen concentrators, refrigeration, mobility equipment and cooling or heating.

procedures: During intake and assessment (SVC-02), the intake nurse or supervisor rates the client's disaster risk as high, moderate or low, noting oxygen or other powered equipment, limited mobility, cognitive impairment, living alone, lack of transportation and pets or other dependents.

The supervisor records at least two emergency contacts, the client's physician if the client wishes to share it, medical conditions and allergies the client agrees to share, medication list location and any evacuation help available from family, neighbors or others. The information goes in the client record (RR-01) and the service plan (SVC-03).

The supervisor reviews with the client or representative a simple emergency plan: where to go, what to take, how to leave the home, who will help and what to do if power is lost. The plan is reviewed again at each service plan update.

The Administrator maintains a priority call list sorted by risk rating and updated at least quarterly and whenever a client starts, stops or changes condition. The list is available electronically and in print at the office and with the after-hours coordinator.

The agency staffs an after-hours coordinator line at [PHONE]. Aides and clients are given this number in writing at intake or orientation. The coordinator has access to the priority call list, aide roster and emergency contacts.

At orientation and annually, aides complete training on emergency procedures, including calling 911, basic safety precautions, what to do in a fire or earthquake and how to respond to a power outage (HSC §1796.44(b)).

In a medical emergency, the aide calls 911, stays with the client, gives help within the aide's scope, notifies the supervisor and then the emergency contacts, and completes an incident report under SAF-03.

When a wildfire, earthquake, power shutoff, heat event or other disaster is announced or occurs, the Administrator activates the disaster plan, assigns staff to contact high-risk clients first and records every contact attempt and outcome.

Aides on duty during a disaster follow the client's emergency plan, move the client to safety where it can be done without lifting beyond safe limits (SAF-06), call 911 if needed and call the coordinator as soon as it is safe. Aides are not required to stay in a location where their own safety is in immediate danger.

If aides cannot reach clients, the coordinator reassigns available aides, uses the backup staffing roster and contacts family members or emergency contacts. If a high-risk client cannot be reached, the coordinator asks local law enforcement or fire services to check on the client where this is available.

During power shutoffs and heat events, the supervisor or aide checks that medical equipment has battery or backup power, medications are properly stored, the client is hydrated and the home is a safe temperature. The supervisor offers help locating a cooling or warming location.
The Administrator informs clients and representatives of any expected disruption to services and documents the contacts. Missed visits during a disaster follow SVC-06.
After the event, the Administrator holds a debrief within 14 days to review what worked, what failed and any needed changes, and records the results through the quality program (GOV-04).
The Administrator reviews this policy, the priority call list process and the backup staffing plan at least annually and updates them through GOV-03.

responsibilities.duty: Rate each client's risk, record emergency contacts and evacuation help and review the emergency plan with the client.
Know the client's emergency plan, call 911 in life-threatening situations, protect personal safety and report to the coordinator.
Keep the priority call list current, staff the after-hours line, activate the disaster plan, arrange backup staffing and lead the debrief.

documentation: Disaster risk rating and emergency contacts in each client record
Written emergency plan reviewed with client or representative
Priority call list with revision dates
After-hours coordinator log
Disaster activation log with every contact attempt and outcome
Training records for emergency procedures
Post-event debrief notes and annual policy review

policies.title: Caregiver Safety in the Home and Workplace Violence
policies.applies_to: All affiliated home care aides, supervisors, schedulers, office staff and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To protect aides and staff from injury, violence, aggression and unsafe conditions in client homes and at the office, and to give aides clear authority to leave an unsafe situation.
policies.policy: Aides complete safety training at entry, including basic safety precautions and emergency procedures, before being present with a client (HSC §1796.44(b)). The agency maintains workers' compensation coverage for aides (HSC §1796.42(b)). California employers have workplace violence prevention and Injury and Illness Prevention Program obligations. Whether and how these apply to Home Care Organizations has not been confirmed in this manual, so the Administrator will have counsel confirm the applicable requirements and update this policy through GOV-03. Any aide may leave an unsafe situation, including a hostile household member, weapons or aggression, and call 911 and the supervisor. [AGENCY NAME] has a no-retaliation rule for aides who leave or refuse an unsafe assignment in good faith. The agency provides a safe-lifting protocol and a no-lone-lift rule for dependent transfers. Where an aide has occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious material, the OSHA bloodborne pathogens standard (29 CFR 1910.1030) applies and SAF-04 is followed.

definitions.definition: Any act or threat of physical violence, harassment, intimidation or other threatening behavior directed at an aide or staff member at a client's home, in a vehicle or at the office.

A household member who is hostile, intoxicated or aggressive, the presence of weapons displayed or used threateningly, threats, sexual harassment, hazardous conditions or a client's behavior that creates a risk of harm.
An aide may not lift or transfer a dependent client alone when the client cannot bear weight or help, and must use equipment or additional help.
The written method for lifts, transfers and repositioning that uses assistive equipment, body mechanics and the client's service plan.
Injury and Illness Prevention Program, the written program California employers are generally required to maintain. Its applicability to HCOs will be confirmed with counsel.

procedures: At orientation and before client contact, each aide completes safety training that covers basic safety precautions, emergency procedures and infection control (HSC §1796.44(b)). Training also covers how to recognize and defuse aggression, safe lifting and the rules in this policy. Completion is recorded in the personnel record (PER-03, PER-05).

During intake and assessment (SVC-02), the supervisor completes a home safety screen noting weapons the client discloses, aggressive household members, pets, hazards, lighting and parking, history of aggression, substance use in the home and any prior threats or harassment. Identified risks are recorded in the service plan (SVC-03) with steps to reduce them.
Before the first visit, the scheduler gives the aide the address, the client's contact, the supervisor's number [PHONE] and the after-hours line, and tells the aide about any recorded safety concern.

An aide who feels unsafe at any time may leave the home immediately. The aide goes to a safe location, calls 911 if there is immediate danger and then calls the supervisor. The aide does not need permission to leave and is not required to explain more until safe.

The aide does not stay if a household member is threatening, intoxicated and aggressive, displays or uses a weapon, or sexually harasses the aide. The aide does not argue, block anyone or try to take a weapon.

The supervisor responds immediately by phone, checks on the aide's safety and decides how to protect the client, including calling emergency services or arranging a safe replacement. The supervisor does not require the aide to return to the home until the Administrator has reviewed the situation.

The aide completes an incident report within 24 hours (SAF-03). The Administrator reviews every violence or safety incident within 2 business days, decides on changes such as paired visits, daytime-only visits, a change of staffing or discharge under SVC-09, and documents the decision. The agency does not abandon a client in danger and follows SVC-09 and SAF-01 where required.
If a client or household member is harming, neglecting or exploiting the client, the aide or supervisor also reports under SAF-01. If a child is at risk, SAF-02 applies.

No aide is disciplined, denied hours or otherwise retaliated against for leaving an unsafe situation in good faith, for reporting a safety concern or for refusing an unsafe task. Any aide who believes retaliation occurred may report it to the Administrator at [PHONE].

Lifting and transfers follow the service plan and the safe-lifting protocol. Aides never lift a dependent client alone if the client cannot bear weight or assist. If the plan calls for a lift the aide cannot safely do, the aide stops, uses equipment or a second person and notifies the supervisor. Any change to the transfer method is recorded in the service plan (SVC-03). Aides do not perform tasks outside SVC-01.
Aides use gloves and other PPE and follow the exposure procedures in SAF-04 for blood or body fluid exposure, including needlestick injuries. Contact the supervisor immediately after any exposure.
Aides who drive for work follow SAF-07 and PER-10. Aides do not enter a home alone at night where a safety concern has been recorded unless the supervisor has approved a plan, such as check-in calls.

Aide injuries are handled under PER-12. The supervisor makes sure the aide receives medical care, the incident report is completed and the workers' compensation claim is opened under the policy the agency must maintain (HSC §1796.42(b)).

Office safety: the Administrator keeps the office secure, controls client and visitor access, trains office staff to handle threatening callers and visitors, posts emergency numbers and runs at least one office emergency drill per year.

The Administrator will have counsel confirm which California workplace violence prevention and Injury and Illness Prevention Program requirements apply to the agency, and will update this policy and the training through GOV-03. The Administrator reviews all safety incidents quarterly for trends and reports them through the quality program (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Complete safety training, use safe-lifting methods, follow the service plan, leave unsafe situations, call 911 and the supervisor and file a report within 24 hours.
Complete the home safety screen, respond immediately to safety calls, protect client and aide and enforce the no-lone-lift rule.
Review incidents, prevent retaliation, maintain workers' compensation coverage, confirm applicable workplace safety requirements with counsel and keep the office secure.

documentation: Safety training records for each aide
Home safety screen and service plan safety notes
Incident reports of violence, threats or safety concerns
Administrator review and decision notes
Lifting and transfer instructions in the service plan
Workers' compensation claim reference where an aide is injured
Quarterly safety trend review and annual policy review

policies.title: Transporting Clients
policies.applies_to: All affiliated home care aides who drive clients or drive on client errands, schedulers, supervisors and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To make sure that any transportation [AGENCY NAME] provides is a planned, authorized service delivered by trained, properly licensed and insured aides, and that aides are reimbursed for the mileage they drive for clients.
policies.policy: Transportation is a home care service under HSC §1796.12(n), and [AGENCY NAME] provides it only when it is written into the client's service agreement and service plan. Only an affiliated aide who holds a valid driver's license, current vehicle registration and current auto insurance, and who has completed the annual training on safe client transport (HSC §1796.44(c)), may drive a client. Aides may not transport a client in unsafe conditions, may not use a phone while driving, and may not transport a wheelchair user unless trained in securement and the vehicle can secure the wheelchair. Mileage for client transport and client errands is reimbursed under Labor Code §2802; the 2026 IRS rate of 72.5 cents per mile is the benchmark. [AGENCY NAME] will have counsel and its insurer confirm in writing how the organization's liability coverage and each aide's personal auto coverage apply to client transport. Specific California vehicle-insurance limits have not been verified for this manual.

definitions.definition: Driving a client, in the aide's vehicle or another approved vehicle, to appointments, shopping, social outings or other destinations as authorized in the service plan.
Driving, without the client, to shop, pick up items or conduct other tasks for the client as authorized in the service plan.
Proper restraint of a wheelchair or mobility device and its occupant in a vehicle designed or equipped for that purpose, using a method the aide has been trained to use.
A person 18 or older who is employed by the HCO and is listed on the CDSS Home Care Aide Registry (HSC §1796.12(a)).

procedures: The intake coordinator records during assessment (SVC-02) whether the client needs or wants transportation and lists the destinations, frequency and mobility needs (walker, wheelchair, transfer assistance).

The Administrator or designee confirms transportation is included in the signed service agreement (CR-06) and written into the service plan (SVC-03) before any aide drives a client. Transport not in the plan is not provided.

The scheduler assigns transport only to aides who are on the approved driver list. An aide is added to the list only after the Administrator verifies and files a copy of the aide's valid driver's license, current vehicle registration and proof of current auto insurance (PER-05).

The Administrator obtains written confirmation from counsel and the insurer that [AGENCY NAME]'s general and professional liability coverage (GOV-06) and the aide's personal auto policy apply to client transport and client errands. The confirmation is filed in the compliance binder. Until it is on file, [AGENCY NAME] does not offer client transport.

The Administrator reviews each driver's license, registration and insurance at hire, at least annually, and whenever an expiration date passes. An aide whose documents lapse is removed from driving duties the same day and may not drive until current documents are filed.

Every aide who may drive completes training on how to transport a client safely as part of annual training (PER-03). The training log shows the date and trainer. An aide with no documented transport training does not drive clients.

Before each trip, the aide checks that the vehicle is in safe working condition (tires, lights, brakes, seat belts, clean interior), that the client is seated and buckled, and that mobility aids are stowed or secured safely.
The aide confirms the destination and route with the client, allows enough time, and does not take unplanned stops or detours that are not in the service plan.

The aide must not drive if impaired by alcohol, drugs, medication, illness or fatigue, or in conditions the aide judges unsafe (for example severe weather or a vehicle problem). The aide calls the supervisor, who arranges an alternative, reschedules or helps the client use another transport option.
The aide must not use a handheld or hands-free phone, text or use any device while driving. The aide stops in a safe location before taking a call from the office or the client's family.

Aides may transport a wheelchair user only if the aide has completed securement training and the vehicle can secure the wheelchair. Otherwise the aide does not transport the client and the supervisor arranges another option, such as accessible paratransit or a licensed medical transport provider, and updates the service plan.

Aides may assist a client in and out of the vehicle only as the service plan allows and the aide has been trained to do (SVC-01). The aide does not lift a client beyond the plan or beyond the aide's training.
If the client has a medical emergency during a trip, the aide pulls over safely, calls 911, stays with the client, then notifies the supervisor as soon as it is safe (SVC-08).

For any collision, injury, traffic stop involving the client, or client behavior or condition that made the trip unsafe, the aide reports to the supervisor right away and files an incident report within the timeframe in SAF-03. The Administrator reviews each incident for insurer and CDSS reporting duties (RR-02).
The aide records each trip on the visit record or mileage log with date, client, start and end locations, and odometer or map-verified miles. Logs are submitted with timekeeping (SVC-07).

Payroll reimburses mileage for client transport and client errands under Labor Code §2802, using the current IRS standard mileage rate (72.5 cents per mile for 2026) as the benchmark. Reimbursement is paid with the regular payroll (PER-10).
The Administrator reviews trip logs, incidents and driver documents each quarter as part of quality review (GOV-04) and corrects any gaps.

responsibilities.duty: Approves the driver list, obtains the insurer and counsel confirmation of coverage, reviews driver documents at least annually, and ensures transport is offered only when compliant.
Assigns transport only to approved drivers and only when it is in the service plan.
Confirms transport needs in service plans, arranges alternatives when a trip cannot be done safely, and reviews incident reports.
Keeps license, registration and insurance current, completes transport training, drives safely, avoids phone use, and logs trips and miles.
Reimburses mileage under Labor Code §2802 and keeps the mileage records.

documentation: Approved driver list with copies of license, registration and insurance and the dates checked
Written coverage confirmation from the insurer and counsel
Service agreement and service plan showing transportation authorization
Annual training log entry showing safe transport training and wheelchair securement training, where applicable
Trip and mileage logs and reimbursement records
Incident reports for any transport-related event

policies.title: Registered Home Care Aide Qualifications and Registry Listing
policies.applies_to: Administrator, hiring staff, schedulers and all affiliated home care aides
policies.purpose: To make sure that every person who provides direct care for [AGENCY NAME] clients is a registered, affiliated home care aide who is 18 or older, employed by [AGENCY NAME], listed on the CDSS Home Care Aide Registry and cleared before any client contact.
policies.policy: California uses the term "registered home care aide," not "certified." [AGENCY NAME] allows only affiliated home care aides to provide home care services. An affiliated aide is 18 or older, employed by [AGENCY NAME], and listed on the CDSS Home Care Aide Registry (HSC §1796.12(a)). No aide has direct contact with a client until the aide is cleared on the registry (HSC §1796.43(a)). The Act sets no minimum education or experience and no state competency exam, so [AGENCY NAME] defines job qualifications in written job descriptions (CDSS HCS 281, B2). [AGENCY NAME] verifies each aide's registry status at hire, before assignment and at each renewal.

definitions.definition: The public CDSS website on which registered home care aides are listed (HSC §1796.12(i)).
A person 18 or older who is employed by an HCO and is listed on the registry (HSC §1796.12(a)).
The organization identification number that an aide enters on the registration application to affiliate with [AGENCY NAME].
The CDSS online applicant portal used for Live Scan and home care aide registration.

procedures: The Administrator writes and maintains a job description for the home care aide position, listing duties within the scope in SVC-01, minimum age of 18, required registry listing, and the conditions of employment (fingerprint clearance, criminal-conviction statement, TB clearance and registry listing). The job description is part of the licensing application record (HCS 281, B2).
Recruiting staff verify at application that the candidate is at least 18 and legally able to work, and tell every candidate that employment is conditional on registry listing and clearance.
The Administrator extends a written conditional offer that states the position is as a W-2 employee (PER-08), identifies [AGENCY NAME]'s HCO PIN, and lists the conditions of employment.
The aide registers online through the CDSS Guardian portal or submits form HCS 100 by mail. The fee is $35 per 2 years, with a $35 renewal. The offer letter states who pays the fee.

On the registration application the aide enters [AGENCY NAME]'s HCO PIN so that the aide is affiliated with [AGENCY NAME]. The Administrator confirms the aide has done so and does not give the PIN to anyone not hired by [AGENCY NAME].

The aide completes Live Scan fingerprinting as directed by CDSS (PER-02). The aide may call the Care Provider Management Branch at 1-888-422-5669 or email guardian@dss.ca.gov with registration or Live Scan questions.
The Administrator checks the public CDSS Home Care Aide Registry for the aide's name and status at hire. A dated printout or screenshot is saved in the personnel file.

The scheduler may not place an aide on any client schedule, shadow shift or ride-along until the Administrator has recorded in the personnel file that the aide is cleared and listed, and that entry training is complete (PER-03).
The Administrator rechecks registry status immediately before each aide's first client assignment and records the date and result.
The Administrator tracks each aide's registration expiration date on a renewal calendar and reminds the aide at least 60 days before it. The aide completes the $35 renewal before expiration.
At each renewal, the Administrator verifies on the registry that the aide's listing is current and affiliated with [AGENCY NAME], and files a dated copy.

If an aide's listing lapses, is not renewed, or the registry shows any status other than cleared and listed, the Administrator removes the aide from the schedule the same day, notifies affected clients' supervisors to arrange coverage (SVC-06), and returns the aide to work only after the registry shows the listing is current.
The aide must tell the Administrator immediately of any notice received from CDSS about registry status or clearance.
When an aide leaves, the Administrator completes separation steps and notice to CDSS (PER-11) and updates the aide roster (RR-03).
The Administrator keeps a current roster of all affiliated aides with registry status, PIN affiliation and renewal dates so a complete list can be produced for CDSS on request (RR-03).
At least quarterly, the Administrator audits all active aides against the public registry and records the results (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains job descriptions, verifies registry status at hire, before assignment and at renewal, and removes any aide from the schedule whose listing is not current.
Screen age and work eligibility, issue conditional offers, and explain registration conditions.
Assigns only aides recorded as cleared, listed and trained.
Registers, enters the HCO PIN, renews on time, and reports any CDSS notice about status.

documentation: Job description for home care aide
Offer letter showing the conditions of employment
Dated registry verification at hire, before first assignment and at each renewal
Aide registration and renewal tracking calendar
Quarterly registry audit record
Current aide roster

policies.title: Background Checks and Employee Registries
policies.applies_to: Administrator, hiring staff, aides, office staff, schedulers, supervisors and volunteers
policies.purpose: To make sure no person has contact with clients, prospective clients or confidential client information until all required California background clearance steps are complete.
policies.policy: Aides must be cleared on the CDSS Home Care Aide Registry before direct contact with clients. In addition, any staff person, volunteer or employee who has contact with clients, prospective clients or confidential client information must satisfy HSC §§1796.23, 1796.24, 1796.25, 1796.26 and 1796.28 before that contact or access (HSC §1796.43(a)(1)). [AGENCY NAME] fingerprints applicants by Live Scan through CDSS (Guardian). Employment is conditional on fingerprint clearance, a signed statement of criminal convictions, TB clearance and registry listing (HCS 281, B3). The licensee has passed the background exam under HSC §1796.33 (HSC §1796.37(a)(6)). [AGENCY NAME] does not assign any aide whose status is pending or not cleared. [AGENCY NAME] has counsel confirm the content of the cited sections for the manual's adoption.

definitions.definition: Electronic fingerprinting through which CDSS obtains criminal record information for registration and clearance.
A person whose required CDSS clearance steps are complete and who is shown by CDSS as cleared or listed, as applicable.
A person who has client contact but is not subject to the standard clearance steps; the licensee may require criminal record clearance of such persons (HSC §1796.43(b)).
The criminal record statement form signed by the applicant.

procedures: The Administrator identifies every position, including aides, supervisors, schedulers, office staff and volunteers, and marks whether the position has contact with clients, prospective clients or confidential client information. Any position with that contact or access is a cleared position.

Hiring staff give every applicant for a cleared position a written notice, before the offer, that employment depends on fingerprint clearance, a signed statement of criminal convictions, TB clearance and registry listing for aides.
The applicant signs the criminal record statement (LIC 508) and returns it to the Administrator before the first day of work. A signed statement is placed in the confidential personnel file.

The applicant is fingerprinted by Live Scan through CDSS (Guardian) as directed by the Care Provider Management Branch (1-888-422-5669; guardian@dss.ca.gov). Aides complete Live Scan in connection with their registry application (PER-01).

The Administrator confirms that the §§1796.23, .24, .25, .26 and .28 requirements are satisfied for the person before any contact with clients, prospective clients or confidential client information, including phone contact, scheduling work in the client database and filing client records.

Until clearance is confirmed, the person may not meet or speak with clients or prospective clients, ride along, shadow, or open client records. The person may complete orientation that does not involve clients or confidential information.
The Administrator verifies status through CDSS: for aides, the public registry; for other staff and volunteers, the CDSS clearance notice. A dated copy or screenshot is saved to the personnel file.

Before an aide's first shift, the Administrator re-checks CDSS clearance and registry status, and records the date and result. If status is pending or not cleared, the scheduler may not assign the aide.

If an applicant discloses a conviction, or CDSS reports a result that is not a clearance, the Administrator reviews it with counsel and follows CDSS's determination. The person is not assigned and does not access client information unless and until CDSS clears the person.

If the licensee requires criminal record clearance of an exempt individual who has client contact under HSC §1796.43(b), the Administrator makes the same requirement in writing for everyone in that category and applies it consistently.

If CDSS notifies [AGENCY NAME], or the person reports, a change in clearance status, the Administrator removes the person from client contact and from client information access the same day and documents the action.
The licensee's own background exam under HSC §1796.33 and the Administrator's personnel checks are recorded and available for CDSS review (HSC §1796.37(a)(6)).
The Administrator audits clearance status for all active staff, aides and volunteers at least quarterly and reports exceptions to the governing body (GOV-01, GOV-04).
Background results and conviction statements are kept confidential, are separated from client records, and are shared only with people who need them to carry out this policy (PER-05).

Give notice of conditions, collect signed LIC 508 statements, and send applicants to Live Scan.

policies.title: Orientation, Competency Evaluation and Annual Training
policies.applies_to: Administrator, trainers, supervisors and all affiliated home care aides
policies.purpose: To make sure each aide completes required entry-level and annual training, and demonstrates practical skills, before and while caring for clients.
policies.policy: Each aide completes at least 5 hours of entry-level training before being present with a client: 2 hours of orientation on the aide's role and the terms of employment, and 3 hours of safety training covering basic safety precautions, emergency procedures and infection control (HSC §1796.44(b)). Each aide then completes at least 5 hours of annual training, core-competency and population-specific, which includes clients' rights and safety, daily living needs, reporting, preventing and detecting abuse and neglect, personal hygiene help and other home care services, and safe transport if transportation is provided (HSC §1796.44(c)). From 1/1/2027, annual training must also cover the special care needs of clients with dementia (HSC §1796.44(c)(6)). Training may be online (HSC §1796.44(d)). The Act has no state competency exam; as an operator standard, [AGENCY NAME] requires a skills check-off before an aide performs transfers, incontinence care and safe lifting. [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written training plan that names trainers and objectives and includes a sample training log (HCS 281, B4).

definitions.definition: At least 5 hours completed before presence with a client: 2 hours of orientation and 3 hours of safety training (HSC §1796.44(b)).
At least 5 hours each year of core-competency and population-specific training (HSC §1796.44(c)).
An observed demonstration, signed by a qualified trainer or supervisor, showing the aide can perform a task safely. It is an operator standard, not a state exam.
The written plan of trainers, objectives, topics and sample log submitted with the licensing application (HCS 281, B4).

procedures: The Administrator maintains a written training plan that names each trainer and their qualifications, sets objectives for each topic, and includes a sample training log (HCS 281, B4). The Administrator reviews it at least annually (GOV-03).

Before an aide has any presence with a client, including shadowing, the aide completes the 2-hour orientation on the aide's role and the terms of employment: duties and limits (SVC-01), supervision (SVC-04), pay, schedule, conduct and boundaries (PER-07), and reporting.

Before the same date, the aide completes the 3-hour safety module covering basic safety precautions, emergency procedures and infection control (SAF-04, SAF-05, SAF-08 is not used; SVC-08 for emergencies in the home).
The trainer or supervisor records on the aide's training log the date, topic, hours, delivery method (in person or online) and trainer name. The aide signs the log.
The Administrator confirms in the personnel file that at least 5 hours of entry-level training (2 plus 3) are complete before the scheduler may assign the aide to any client (PER-01).

A supervisor observes and signs a skills check-off for transfers, incontinence care and safe lifting before the aide performs those tasks alone, and records the date. The aide is not assigned clients who need these tasks until the check-off is complete.
The Administrator assigns each aide 5 or more hours of annual training in every 12-month period beginning on the aide's hire date, and tracks the due date on a training calendar.

Annual training covers clients' rights and safety (CR-01); daily living needs; reporting, preventing and detecting abuse and neglect (SAF-01, SAF-02); personal hygiene and other home care services; and safe client transport if [AGENCY NAME] provides transportation (SAF-07).
Training may be delivered online (HSC §1796.44(d)). For online courses, the Administrator keeps the course outline, hours and completion certificate in the training file.
Starting 1/1/2027, the Administrator adds a dementia module on the special care needs of clients with dementia to annual training for every aide (SVC-11). The 5-hour minimums do not change.
As an operator practice, until counsel confirms whether a pre-service dementia component is required, [AGENCY NAME] provides dementia orientation before assigning an aide to a client with dementia.
The Administrator notifies an aide at least 30 days before the annual training due date. If the training is not complete by the due date, the aide is removed from the schedule until it is complete.
Trainers and supervisors also give job-specific coaching when a client's service plan changes (SVC-03).
The Administrator reviews training completion rates and skills check-off results quarterly as part of quality review (GOV-04) and corrects gaps.
Training records are kept in each aide's personnel file (PER-05) and are produced to CDSS on request as proof of compliance with §1796.44 (RR-03).

Deliver training, conduct and sign skills check-offs, and complete training logs.
Completes entry and annual training on time and signs the training log.
Assigns only aides recorded as training-complete.

Online course completion certificates

policies.title: Employee Health and TB Screening
policies.applies_to: Administrator, hiring staff, schedulers and all affiliated home care aides
policies.purpose: To make sure every aide is examined for tuberculosis as the law requires, that no aide with a risk of spreading TB works with clients, and that required certificates are on file.
policies.policy: Each aide hired on or after 1/1/2016 must be examined for TB 90 days before employment or within 7 days after it begins (HSC §1796.45(a)). The exam is a CDC-recommended, FDA-licensed TB infection test and, if the test is positive, a chest X-ray (HSC §1796.45(b)). An aide may not work unless [AGENCY NAME] has documentation from a licensed medical professional that the aide has no risk of spreading disease (HSC §1796.45(b)). A negative result must be repeated at least every 2 years; once a positive test has been followed by an X-ray, repeat exams are no longer required (HSC §1796.45(c)). After each exam the aide gives [AGENCY NAME] the practitioner's certificate, which stays on file (HSC §1796.45(d)). The exam is a condition of initial and continuing employment (HSC §1796.45(e)). [AGENCY NAME] does not impose other health screening requirements unless counsel confirms them.

definitions.definition: A CDC-recommended, FDA-licensed test for tuberculosis infection (HSC §1796.45(b)).
Written documentation from a licensed medical professional of the exam and that the aide has no risk of spreading disease.
An aide moving to [AGENCY NAME] from another HCO.

procedures: Hiring staff tell each applicant in the conditional offer that a TB exam under HSC §1796.45 is a condition of initial and continuing employment, and explain the timing.

The aide has the TB infection test no earlier than 90 days before the start of employment, or within 7 days after the start. Test timing is calculated from the aide's hire date and entered on the TB tracker.
The aide gives [AGENCY NAME] the practitioner's certificate promptly after the exam. The Administrator checks that it identifies the test, the date, and the licensed medical professional.

If the test is positive, the aide must have a chest X-ray. The aide may not work until [AGENCY NAME] holds documentation from a licensed medical professional that the aide has no risk of spreading the disease.

If the aide has not had the exam by the end of day 7 after employment begins, or has no certificate on file, the scheduler removes the aide from all client assignments until the certificate is received.
For an aide with a negative test, the Administrator sets the next due date as no later than 2 years after the last exam and calendars a reminder at least 60 days earlier.
For an aide who had a positive test followed by an X-ray, the Administrator notes this on the tracker and does not require repeat exams, and keeps the original certificate on file.

A transferring aide may meet the requirement with a practitioner's certificate dated within the past 2 years, or with verification from the prior HCO that it holds the certificate and provides a copy before the aide starts (HSC §1796.45(f)). The Administrator files the verification with date and contact name.
Each time a new certificate is received, the Administrator files it in the aide's confidential medical section of the personnel file (PER-05) and updates the tracker.
If an aide's repeat exam is overdue, the Administrator notifies the aide in writing and the scheduler removes the aide from client assignments until the certificate is on file.

An aide who develops symptoms of TB or is told by a health provider that there is a risk of spreading disease must tell the Administrator immediately, and does not work until a licensed medical professional documents no risk of spreading disease.
Payment for the exam and certificate is decided by the Administrator with counsel and stated in the offer letter.
The Administrator does not add any other health screening requirement for aides unless counsel confirms it is permitted, and does not ask for medical details beyond what the certificate shows.
TB certificates and the tracker are kept confidential and produced to CDSS on request as proof of compliance with §1796.45 (RR-03).

responsibilities.duty: Tracks exam dates, reviews certificates, keeps them on file, and removes non-compliant aides from the schedule.
Notify applicants of the TB condition and collect certificates.
Does not assign any aide without a current certificate on file.
Completes the exam on time, repeats as required, and gives each certificate to [AGENCY NAME].

documentation: Practitioner's TB certificate after each exam
TB tracker with exam dates and next due dates
Positive-test follow-up documentation (X-ray and no-risk statement)
Transfer verification from prior HCO
Written notices of overdue exams and schedule removals

policies.title: Personnel Records
policies.applies_to: Administrator, hiring staff, payroll and office staff who handle personnel files
policies.purpose: To keep complete, confidential and retrievable personnel records that show each aide meets state requirements and that can be produced to CDSS on request.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a personnel file for each aide containing registry status and PIN, Live Scan clearance, TB certificates, entry-level and annual training logs, the signed criminal-conviction statement, Form I-9 and payroll records. On CDSS request, [AGENCY NAME] provides a complete list of affiliated aides and proof that each aide meets HSC §§1796.43, 1796.44 and 1796.45 (HSC §1796.37(a)(5)). TB certificates must stay on file (HSC §1796.45(d)). The Act sets no retention period, and California Labor Code record rules have not been verified for this manual, so [AGENCY NAME] adopts a retention schedule with counsel. Personnel files are confidential, kept separate from client records, and available for CDSS inspection.

definitions.definition: The set of records for one employee showing qualifications, clearance, training, health certificates and employment and payroll documents.
The written schedule, set with counsel, stating how long each type of personnel record is kept.
The federal Employment Eligibility Verification form.

procedures: The Administrator opens a personnel file for each aide at the conditional offer, using a standard checklist of required contents.

The file is divided into sections: hiring and registry (job description acknowledgment, registry verification and PIN, Live Scan clearance, signed conviction statement); training (entry and annual logs, skills check-offs); health (TB certificates, kept in a confidential section); employment (offer letter, W-2 status, signed policies); and payroll.
Hiring staff complete Form I-9 with the aide under the federal timing rules and keep the I-9 in a separate I-9 folder, and not in the general file, if counsel advises that practice.

The Administrator confirms before the aide's first client assignment that the file shows registry listing, Live Scan clearance, TB certificate and 5 hours of entry-level training (PER-01, PER-02, PER-03, PER-04).
Each time a new document is received (registry renewal, TB certificate, training record), staff file it within 5 business days and update the compliance tracker.
The Administrator uses a quarterly checklist audit of every file for missing or expired items and records corrections (GOV-04).
The Administrator keeps the current list of affiliated aides (RR-03) so a complete list and proof that each aide meets §§1796.43, 1796.44 and 1796.45 can be given to CDSS on request.
When CDSS asks for the aide list or proof, the Administrator provides it within the time CDSS states, keeps a copy of what was sent, and records the date and CDSS contact (GOV-07).

Personnel files are stored in a locked cabinet or access-controlled electronic system, separate from client records, and only the Administrator, designee and payroll staff with a need to know may access them.
Medical information such as TB certificates is kept in a confidential section and is not shared with other staff or clients.
The Administrator, with counsel, adopts a written retention schedule of [RETENTION PERIOD SET WITH COUNSEL] for each record type, and notes that TB certificates stay on file under HSC §1796.45(d).

When an aide separates, the Administrator completes the separation steps (PER-11), keeps the file for the full retention period, and does not destroy any record until the schedule allows and no inspection, complaint or legal hold applies.
Records are destroyed by shredding or secure electronic deletion, and the Administrator logs the date and category destroyed.
The aide may review the aide's own file on written request, and the Administrator sets a time within [NUMBER OF DAYS SET WITH COUNSEL] to respond.

responsibilities.duty: Owns the personnel file system, audits files quarterly, adopts the retention schedule with counsel and responds to CDSS requests.
Build files from the checklist, complete the I-9 and file new documents promptly.
Keep payroll records and file them within the personnel system.
Reviews audit results and ensures resources for record-keeping.
